The raw quadrature rule below takes the continuous input function, including any off-grid values used by a local term or pointwise lifting. It is not by itself asserted to factor through its stored input samples. A finite-sampling version is specified after the raw rule.

For the continuous-function architecture, take its pointwise lift $P$, layers indexed by $0\le t<L$, and pointwise projection $Q$. Given a finite partition of $D$ into nonempty measurable cells $E_1,\dots,E_N$, choose tags $\xi_j\in E_j$ and weights $\omega_j=|E_j|$. Initialize the raw lifted field $v_{0,n}(x)=P(a(x))$ on $\bar D$ and store $v_{0,n}(\xi_j)$. For each layer whose output domain is $\bar D$, define at every $x\in\bar D$
$$v_{t+1,n}(x)=\sigma_t\!\left(W_tv_{t,n}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\kappa_t(x,\xi_j)v_{t,n}(\xi_j)+b_t(x)\right),$$
and store its values at all tags for the next layer. If the last layer instead has output domain $\bar D'\ne\bar D$, use its required zero local term and define, for $x\in\bar D'$,
$$v_{L,n}(x)=\sigma_{L-1}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\kappa_{L-1}(x,\xi_j)v_{L-1,n}(\xi_j)+b_{L-1}(x)\right).$$
Return the function $x\mapsto Q(v_{L,n}(x))$ on the output closure, evaluating these same formulas at each requested query point. A refinement changes cells, tags, and weights, while all layer, lifting, and projection parameters remain fixed.

For a finite-sampling realization on continuous inputs, first reconstruct the input from its prescribed tags by the normalized nonnegative weights in the finite-sampling reconstruction bridge. Run the raw rule on this reconstructed function, including in the pointwise lifting and every local term. Its output is then a function of the finite input sample vector alone, with the same continuum parameters. The weights and reconstruction change with the partition; the learned parameters do not. Along partition sequences whose maximal cell diameters $h_n=\max_j\operatorname{diam}(E_{n,j})$ tend to zero, if the raw maps converge compact-uniformly in the output supremum norm, the bridge transfers that convergence to this finite-sampling realization. For a stronger compatible Banach input/output formulation, supply reconstructions into the actual input Banach space that converge compact-uniformly in that input norm; the same bridge then preserves the raw rule's proved output Banach norm convergence. The explicit continuous-input weights alone do not assert this stronger reconstruction property.

Let $d,d'\in\mathbb N$ with $d,d'\ge1$, let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, and Jordan measurable, let $D'\subset\mathbb R^{d'}$ be nonempty and bounded, let $\kappa\in C(\bar D'\times\bar D)$ be scalar-valued, and let $K\subset C(\bar D)$ be nonempty and compact in the supremum norm. Give products of metric spaces the max metric. Let $Q_n:C(\bar D)\to\mathbb R$ be bounded linear quadrature functionals with $\sup_n\|Q_n\|<\infty$ and $Q_n f\to\int_D f(y)\,dy$ for every $f\in C(\bar D)$. Then
$$\sup_{a\in K}\sup_{x\in\bar D'}\left|Q_n\bigl(\kappa(x,\cdot)a(\cdot)\bigr)-\int_D\kappa(x,y)a(y)\,dy\right|\longrightarrow0.$$
This conclusion is in the supremum norm on the output variable. It does not by itself establish convergence in an arbitrary Banach output norm $U$.

Let $X,U$ be real Banach spaces, and let continuous maps $H,H_n:X\to U$ satisfy $\sup_{a\in K}\|H_n(a)-H(a)\|_U\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Suppose continuous finite-dimensional sampling and reconstruction maps $S_n:X\to E_n$ and $J_n:E_n\to X$ are supplied and satisfy $\sup_{a\in K}\|J_nS_n(a)-a\|_X\to0$ on every such $K$. Then
$$G_n(a)=H_n(J_n(S_n(a)))$$
factors through finite-dimensional data, with $F_n=E_n$, finite map the identity and output reconstruction $R_n=H_n\circ J_n:E_n\to U$, and $G_n\to H$ uniformly on every norm-compact input set in the actual $U$ norm. When $X,U$ are function spaces on bounded domains with the pointwise output convention required by the discretization-invariant-family definition, this is a finite-sampling family in that definition.

For the supremum-norm continuous-input case these reconstruction hypotheses always hold with exactly the prescribed tags of arbitrary finite partitions of a nonempty bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ whose maximal cell diameters $h_n$ tend to zero. Namely let $X=C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$, let $S_n(a)=(a(\xi_{n,j}))_j$, and, when $h_n>0$, for $x\in\bar D$ put
$$w_{n,j}(x)=\max\{0,2h_n-|x-\xi_{n,j}|\},\qquad J_n(z)(x)=\frac{\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)z_j}{\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)}.$$
If $h_n=0$, the domain is the zero-dimensional singleton; define $J_n(z)$ to be the constant function with value $z_1$. This reconstructs every input exactly. In both branches $\|J_nS_n\|_{X\to X}\le1$, and the reconstruction error is bounded by the input modulus of continuity at $2h_n$, uniformly on every compact input family. In a stronger Banach input norm the first clause applies whenever the stated reconstructions converge in that norm; convergence in the supremum norm alone is not substituted for that condition.

A further case needs no input reconstruction. Suppose a raw finite architecture first uses its input only through the sampled pointwise lift in the integral-only field $v_{1,n}(x)=\sum_j\omega_{n,j}\kappa_n(x,\xi_{n,j})P(a(\xi_{n,j}))+b_n(x)$, and every later stage acts on this field and the fixed parameters without further access to the original input. Assume these stages are defined and continuous on the compatible Banach spaces in question. Then each raw map itself factors through the finite input sample vector. Its compact-uniform raw convergence therefore already gives a finite-sampling family in the actual output norm, regardless of whether a sample reconstruction into the input norm has been supplied. This includes the integral-only universality subclass, when its kernels and intermediate spaces satisfy the declared compatible norm hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Write $I(v)=\int_D\kappa(\cdot,y)v(y)\,dy$ for one compatible Banach layer, and let $C$ be a compact subset of its input space $X$. Its image in $C(\bar D)$ is compact: pulling an open cover back through the continuous inclusion and using compactness proves this directly. Thus $R=\sup_{v\in C}\|v\|_\infty<\infty$. This family has a common modulus of continuity tending to zero. Indeed a finite $\eta$-net in the supremum norm and uniform continuity of its finitely many functions give $|v(y)-v(z)|\le2\eta+\max_j|v_j(y)-v_j(z)|$ for every $v\in C$. Uniform continuity of the finitely many functions follows by the compact-domain subsequence contradiction. Let $B=\sup_y\|\kappa(\cdot,y)\|_{\mathcal L(\mathbb R^q,Y)}$ and let $\omega_\kappa$ be its norm modulus. Compactness similarly proves $B<\infty$ and $\omega_\kappa(h)\to0$. Therefore the $Y$-valued integrands $\Phi_v(y)=\kappa(\cdot,y)v(y)$ have common modulus bounded by $R\omega_\kappa(h)+B\omega_C(h)$.

A continuous $Y$-valued function $\Phi$ on $\bar D$ has an integral in $Y$: volume-weighted step sums on partitions of diameter $h$ form a Cauchy family, since comparing two sums on their common refinement bounds their difference by $|D|\omega_\Phi(h+h')$. Completeness of $Y$ gives a limit, independent of tags and partitions. Each coordinate of point evaluation on $Y$ is bounded by its specified continuous inclusion into $C(\bar D';\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}})$; explicitly, $|u_j(x)|\le c_Y\|u\|_Y$. Applying these bounded functionals to the convergent sums therefore identifies the limit with the pointwise integral in every coordinate. Comparing a fixed tagged sum to refinements and taking the limit gives $\|Q_n(v)-I(v)\|_Y\le |D|[R\omega_\kappa(h_n)+B\omega_C(h_n)]$ uniformly for $v\in C$. Also $\|Q_n(v)-Q_n(w)\|_Y\le |D|B\|v-w\|_\infty\le |D|Bc_X\|v-w\|_X$, where $c_X$ is the embedding bound. These estimates use only measurable disjoint cells, their volumes summing to $|D|$, and their diameter bound.

Suppose inductively that the discrete inputs $v_n(a)$ converge in $X$ to the continuum inputs $v(a)$ uniformly for $a$ in the original compact set $K$. The continuum map is continuous by the bound for $I$ from step 2.1 and continuity of all other maps, so $C=v(K)$ is compact. Comparing preactivations at $v_n(a)$ and $v(a)$, the quadrature Lipschitz bound and the bounded local-map norm give an upper bound $(|D|Bc_X+\|W\|)\|v_n(a)-v(a)\|_X+\|Q_n(v(a))-I(v(a))\|_Y$, which tends to zero uniformly in $a$. The continuum preactivations form a compact set $P\subset Y$. A continuous map $T:Y\to X'$ takes perturbations tending uniformly to zero around $P$ to uniformly vanishing output errors: for a prescribed $\varepsilon$, cover $P$ by finitely many balls $B(p_i,r_i)$ on each of which $\|T(z)-T(p_i)\|<\varepsilon/2$ for $\|z-p_i\|<3r_i$, and use a positive perturbation bound smaller than $\min_i r_i$. If $p\in B(p_i,r_i)$ and $\|z-p\|<\min_i r_i$, both images are within $\varepsilon/2$ of $T(p_i)$. Apply this to the activation. The same argument treats continuous lifting or projection maps. Starting with the identical input and proceeding through the finitely many stages proves uniform convergence in the final Banach norm.

For the supremum-norm architecture take every relevant $X$ and $Y$ to be the continuous-function space with its supremum norm. Joint continuity of $\kappa(x,y)$ on the compact product implies continuity of $y\mapsto\kappa(\cdot,y)$ in that norm, by its uniform modulus on the product. Finite matrix local terms are bounded in that norm. For any fixed continuous scalar activation, its induced map on continuous functions is continuous in the supremum norm: near a function of norm $R$, all scalar arguments lie in $[-R-1,R+1]$, where the activation is uniformly continuous. Pointwise finite networks are finite compositions of these continuous maps. Thus all conditions in steps 1.1–2.1 hold, proving the first clause and then its continuously embedded input-space version.

Each raw map is continuous between its specified spaces: finite quadrature sums use bounded point evaluations and bounded kernel maps, and all local, activation, lifting and projection maps are continuous by hypothesis. For continuous inputs, apply the explicit reconstructions in [F3]; steps 1.1–4.1 supply the raw compact-uniform convergence required there. The bridge gives finite-dimensional sampling and output reconstruction with the same continuum parameters and output supremum convergence. In the general Banach case use the supplied reconstructions converging in its actual input norm and apply the first clause of the same bridge; its compact-union argument preserves exactly the output norm proved in step 3.1. For an integral-only first layer after a general lifting $P$, define $S_n(a)=(P(a)(\xi_{n,j}))_j$. For an arbitrary vector $z$ in this finite-dimensional space, form the first field $\sum_j\omega_{n,j}\kappa(\cdot,\xi_{n,j})z_j+b$ and apply all subsequent stages to define $R_n(z)$. Compatibility makes this a continuous output-valued map, and the raw map equals $R_nS_n$ exactly. This is the construction of [F3], with the lifted field as input. A pointwise lift computes $S_n$ from the original input samples; a nonlocal lift need not do so. The explicitly specified sampling map and identity finite map give the asserted discretization family in either case.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, let $\Gamma\subseteq\partial U$ be closed, let $L$ be a differential operator on $U$, and let $B$ be a boundary operator on $\Gamma$. Let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and $g:\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ be target data. For a trial function $h$, define its residuals by $r_h(x)=L[h](x)-f(x)$ and $q_h(x)=B[h](x)-g(x)$. For $0<\alpha\le1$ and a function $v$ on a set $E$, define its Hölder seminorm by
$$[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}\frac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
Set $[v]_{\alpha;E}=0$ when $E$ has fewer than two points. Only trial functions for which $L[h]$ on $U$ and $B[h]$ on $\Gamma$ are pointwise defined and finite are admitted. For the population loss, require $f,r_h$ to be measurable with respect to $(U,\mu_r)$ and $g,q_h$ to be measurable with respect to $(\Gamma,\mu_b)$. For positive fixed weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$ and probability measures $\mu_r$ on $U$, $\mu_b$ on $\Gamma$, the population loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|r_h|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|q_h|^2\,d\mu_b.$$
These nonnegative population integrals take values in $[0,+\infty]$, so they may be infinite. The Hölder seminorms below may likewise be infinite.

For $d\ge2$, given positive integer counts $m_r,m_b$, residual collocation points $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}$, and boundary collocation points $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}$, the empirical loss is
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_{m}(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|r_h(x_r^i)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|q_h(x_b^j)|^2.$$
For $d=1$, a bounded Lipschitz domain has finite boundary, so $\Gamma$ is finite. In this branch require every singleton $\{y\}\subseteq\Gamma$ to be $\mu_b$-measurable. When every point of $\Gamma$ is available deterministically, define its exact full-boundary contribution by
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)=\lambda_b\sum_{y\in\Gamma}\mu_b(\{y\})|q_h(y)|^2=\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|q_h|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
and, for a positive integer count $m_r$ and residual collocation points $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}$, set
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_{m}(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|r_h(x_r^i)|^2+\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b).$$
For $d\ge2$, its Hölder-regularized version is
$$\operatorname{Loss}_{m}(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)=\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^{2}+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^{2}.$$
For $d=1$, the Hölder-regularized version is
$$\operatorname{Loss}_{m}(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)=\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^{2};$$
it uses the exact full-boundary contribution above, has no random boundary sample, and has no boundary seminorm penalty. Require the regularization coefficients appearing in either version to be nonnegative; a zero coefficient contributes zero even when its seminorm is infinite. For finite realized sample lists the empirical sums are finite; the regularized objective is allowed to take the value $+\infty$. These are population and empirical functionals; they do not specify an optimization algorithm or assert that training reaches a global minimizer.

Inputs are a dimension $d\ge1$, the data and operators specified in the physics-informed residual loss definition, $0<\alpha\le1$, positive weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$, and an admissible trial function $h$. The procedure returns the scalar empirical objective value $J_m(h)$. It uses the realized sample points and target values as inputs; it does not generate random samples.

For $d\ge2$, also supply positive integer counts $m_r,m_b$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with their observed values $f(x_r^i)$, boundary samples $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}\in\Gamma$ with their observed values $g(x_b^j)$, constants $c_r,c_b,C_r,C_b>0$, and small-scale cutoffs $\ell_{0,i},\rho_{0,i}>0$. At the selected partition scales $0<\ell_i\le\ell_{0,i}$, require cells $U_j^{\ell_r}$ and $\Gamma_j^{\ell_b}$ with masses at least $c_r\ell_r^d$ and $c_b\ell_b^{d-1}$, each contained in a cube of side $\ell_i$. Require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho^d$ and $\mu_b(\overline B_\rho(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\rho^{d-1}$ for every center and for all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,i}$. The admissible counts satisfy, for $i\in\{r,b\}$,
$$m_i\ge\max\{1,c_i^{-2}\ell_{0,i}^{-2s_i},c_i^{-2}d^{s_i}\rho_{0,i}^{-2s_i}\},$$
so the computed partition scales and fill radii lie in the specified ranges.

For $d=1$, supply a positive integer $m_r$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with observed values $f(x_r^i)$, constants $c_r,C_r>0$, and cutoffs $\ell_{0,r},\rho_{0,r}>0$. At the residual scale $\ell_r$ below, require a finite measurable partition with each cell contained in an interval of length $\ell_r$ and mass at least $c_r\ell_r$, and require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho$ for every center $x\in U$ and all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,r}$. The admissible count satisfies
$$m_r\ge\max\{1,c_r^{-2}\ell_{0,r}^{-2},c_r^{-2}\rho_{0,r}^{-2}\},$$
so $\ell_r=\delta_r$ is in the specified ranges. Supply the observed boundary values at every point of the finite set $\Gamma$ with their masses $\mu_b(\{y\})$. No random boundary sample or boundary sample count is used.

For $d\ge2$, set $s_r=d$, $s_b=d-1$, and, for $i\in\{r,b\}$, compute
$$\ell_i=(c_i\sqrt{m_i})^{-1/s_i},\qquad \delta_i=\sqrt d\,\ell_i,\qquad \kappa_i=C_i/c_i,$$
$$C_m=3\max_{i\in\{r,b\}}\{\kappa_i d^{s_i/2}m_i^{1/2}\},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}=\frac{3\lambda_i\delta_i^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
For $d=1$, compute
$$\ell_r=\delta_r=(c_r\sqrt{m_r})^{-1},\qquad \kappa_r=C_r/c_r,\qquad C_m=3\kappa_r m_r^{1/2},$$
$$\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\delta_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m} =\frac{\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha}}{\kappa_r}m_r^{-\alpha-1/2},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=0.$$
For $d\ge2$, use supplied regularization weights $\lambda^R_{i,m}$ satisfying $\lambda^R_{i,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}$ componentwise; for a sequence of sample counts also require $\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty=O(\|\widehat\lambda_m^R\|_\infty)$. For $d=1$, set $\lambda^R_{b,m}=0$ and choose $\lambda^R_{r,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}$, with the corresponding one-coordinate max-norm order condition across a sequence of counts. If no residual weights are supplied, set them equal to their thresholds.

Finally evaluate and return $J_m(h)=\operatorname{Loss}_m(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)$ using the realized residual values, the realized boundary values when $d\ge2$, the exact weighted full-boundary contribution when $d=1$, and the residual seminorm penalty when $d=1$ or both seminorm penalties when $d\ge2$. The regularization thresholds are the source's exact thresholds and cannot be replaced by a generic positive penalty.

For $d\ge2$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^d$ be measurable, and let $\mu_r$ and $\mu_b$ be probability measures on them. For positive integers $m_r,m_b$, let the residual samples $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ and boundary samples $x_1^b,\ldots,x_{m_b}^b$ form $\varepsilon_r$- and $\varepsilon_b$-nets of $U$ and $\Gamma$ in Euclidean distance. Assume that for every center $x\in U$ and $y\in\Gamma$,
$$\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r^d,\qquad \mu_b(\overline B_{\varepsilon_b}(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}.$$
Suppose $[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}$, $[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$, $[f]_{\alpha;U}$, and $[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$ are finite, where $[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, with value zero when $E$ has fewer than two points. Let $\lambda_r,\lambda_b>0$, and use the population and empirical weighted-square PINN losses
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|L[h]-f|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|B[h](x_j^b)-g(x_j^b)|^2.$$

$$C_m=3\max\{C_rm_r\varepsilon_r^d,\ C_bm_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}\},\quad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\quad \lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
Then

and the empirical loss $\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)$. Set

$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2.$$
There is no random boundary term or boundary-data error term in this branch because the full boundary contribution is evaluated exactly.

Let $d\ge1$, $s>0$, and let $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ carry a probability measure $\mu$. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and $c>0$, and put $\varepsilon=(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}$. Suppose there is a finite measurable partition $X_1,\ldots,X_K$ of $X$ at this particular scale such that each cell lies in a cube of side $\varepsilon$ and $\mu(X_j)\ge c\varepsilon^s$. Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be independent random points each with law $\mu$. Then with probability at least
$$1-\sqrt m\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt m}\right)^m$$
every point of $X$ lies within Euclidean distance $\sqrt d\,c^{-1/s}m^{-1/(2s)}$ of at least one sample point. For an interior space of dimension $d$, use $s=d$; for a boundary space of Hausdorff dimension $d-1>0$, use $s=d-1$ and its own cell-mass constant. If $d=1$ and every boundary point is available deterministically, the boundary fill distance is zero and no random boundary sample is needed.

For $d\ge2$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^d$ be measurable, and let $\mu_r$ and $\mu_b$ be probability measures on them. For positive integers $m_r,m_b$, let the residual samples $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ and boundary samples $x_1^b,\ldots,x_{m_b}^b$ form $\varepsilon_r$- and $\varepsilon_b$-nets of $U$ and $\Gamma$ in Euclidean distance. Assume that for every center $x\in U$ and $y\in\Gamma$,
$$\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r^d,\qquad \mu_b(\overline B_{\varepsilon_b}(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}.$$
Suppose $[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}$, $[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$, $[f]_{\alpha;U}$, and $[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}$ are finite, where $[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{x\ne y\in E}|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, with value zero when $E$ has fewer than two points. Let $\lambda_r,\lambda_b>0$, and use the population and empirical weighted-square PINN losses
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)=\lambda_r\int_U|L[h]-f|^2\,d\mu_r+\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b,$$
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\frac{\lambda_b}{m_b}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}|B[h](x_j^b)-g(x_j^b)|^2.$$
Define
$$C_m=3\max\{C_rm_r\varepsilon_r^d,\ C_bm_b\varepsilon_b^{d-1}\},\quad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\quad \lambda^R_{b,m}=\frac{3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\left(\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+\lambda^R_{b,m}[B[h]]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2\right)+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_b\varepsilon_b^{2\alpha}[g]_{\alpha;\Gamma}^2.$$

For $d=1$, assume $\mu_r$ is a probability measure on measurable $U\subset\mathbb R$, and $\Gamma$ is a nonempty finite measurable set with probability measure $\mu_b$, with every singleton $\{y\}\subseteq\Gamma$ measurable. Every point of $\Gamma$ is available deterministically. For a positive integer $m_r$, let $x_1^r,\ldots,x_{m_r}^r$ form an $\varepsilon_r$-net of $U$, and assume $\mu_r(\overline B_{\varepsilon_r}(x)\cap U)\le C_r\varepsilon_r$ for every center $x\in U$. Suppose the same four Hölder seminorms are finite. Use the exact weighted boundary loss
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)=\lambda_b\int_\Gamma|B[h]-g|^2\,d\mu_b=\lambda_b\sum_{y\in\Gamma}\mu_b(\{y\})|B[h](y)-g(y)|^2$$
and the empirical loss $\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda_r}{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}|L[h](x_i^r)-f(x_i^r)|^2+\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN},b}(h;\lambda_b)$. Set
$$C_m=3C_rm_r\varepsilon_r,\qquad \lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m},\qquad \lambda^R_{b,m}=0.$$
Then
$$\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h;\lambda)\le C_m\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}_m(h;\lambda)+C_m\lambda^R_{r,m}[L[h]]_{\alpha;U}^2+3\lambda_r\varepsilon_r^{2\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;U}^2.$$
There is no random boundary term or boundary-data error term in this branch because the full boundary contribution is evaluated exactly.

Let $X\subset\mathbb R^D$ carry a probability measure $\mu$, let $s,c>0$, and fix an integer $m\ge1$. Put $\ell=(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}$. Suppose a specified finite measurable partition $X_1,\ldots,X_K$ of $X$ has each cell contained in a cube of side $\ell$ and of mass at least $c\ell^s$. Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be independent points of law $\mu$, and put $\delta=\sqrt D\ell$. With probability at least $\max\{0,1-\sqrt m\exp(-\sqrt m/8)\}$ every cell contains at least $\sqrt m/2$ samples, counted with multiplicity. On this event, simultaneously for all real functions $v,g$ with finite $\alpha$-Hölder seminorms on $X$,
$$\|v-g\|_{\infty;X}^2\le6\sqrt m\left(\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2\right)+3\delta^{2\alpha}([v]_{\alpha;X}^2+[g]_{\alpha;X}^2).$$
No independence between the functions and the samples is required.

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $X$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $d\ge1$, let $c>0$, and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $X$. There is no family of finite measurable partitions $\mathcal P_\varepsilon$ of $X$, one for every $\varepsilon>0$, for which every cell $E\in\mathcal P_\varepsilon$ satisfies $\mu(E)\ge c\varepsilon^d$.

For $d\ge2$, $0<\alpha\le1$, and positive constants in equation (3.1), the count condition $m_r=O(m_b^{d/(d-1)})$ alone does not imply that the two threshold coordinates have bounded max-to-min ratio. In particular, choosing $\lambda_m^R=\widehat\lambda_m^R$ satisfies the stated coordinatewise lower bound and norm upper bound, while that ratio can diverge.

derivations.claim: Write $J_m$ for the regularized objective at $h_m$ and $a_i=D^\alpha c_i^{-2\alpha/s_i}$, so $\delta_i^{2\alpha}=a_iA_i$. Minimality against $u_m^*$ and [F1] give $0\le J_m\le M\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty\le K\max\{A_r,A_b\}/C_m$, for a fixed $K$. In particular, the $i$th empirical mean squared error is at most $J_m/\lambda_i$ and the squared operator seminorm is at most $J_m/\lambda^R_{i,m}$. No max-to-min ratio is used.

On both hit-cell events, [F2] and [F3] give $\operatorname{Loss}^{\mathrm{PINN}}(h_m;\lambda)\le C_mJ_m+3\sum_i\lambda_i a_iA_i[\mathrm{data}_i]_{\alpha}^2=O(A_r+A_b)$ by step 1.1. The union bound gives the stated joint probability without an independence premise; independence of the streams gives the product. If $0<c_i\le1$, then $0\le1-1/\sqrt{m_i}\le1-c_i/\sqrt{m_i}$, which proves the stated normalized comparison of probabilities.

On the two occupancy events apply [F4] with $(v,g)=(L[h_m],f)$ and $(B[h_m],g)$ respectively. For each $i$, step 1.1 yields $$\|\mathrm{error}_i\|_\infty^2\le\frac{6\sqrt{m_i}}{\lambda_i}J_m+3a_iA_i\frac{J_m}{\lambda^R_{i,m}}+3a_iA_i[\mathrm{data}_i]_{\alpha}^2\le\left(\frac{6\sqrt{m_i}}{\lambda_i}+\frac{C_m}{\lambda_i}\right)J_m+3a_iA_i[\mathrm{data}_i]_{\alpha}^2.$$ Here $\lambda^R_{i,m}\ge3\lambda_i a_iA_i/C_m$ gives the second inequality. Since $C_m\ge3(C_i/c_i)D^{s_i/2}\sqrt{m_i}$ for each component, step 1.1 makes the last expression $O(A_r+A_b)$. This proves the uniform bound and its event probability. It remains valid for all sample-dependent minimizers because [F4] is simultaneous for every function.

For every integer $n$, $Q(n)=\sqrt n e^{-\sqrt n/8}$. Grouping $k^2\le n<(k+1)^2$ bounds its sum by $\sum_{k\ge1}(2k+1)(k+1)e^{-k/8}<\infty$; convergence follows, for example, since the ratio of successive summands tends to $e^{-1/8}<1$. Apply [F5] separately to the occupancy failure events at every integer sample count in each fixed nested stream. Almost surely, beyond two finite count thresholds every occupancy event holds, so step 2.2 applies along every count pair tending to infinity, including arbitrarily slowly growing or repeated count pairs. Thus both uniform errors tend to zero. Finally $m_r\le C m_b^{D/(D-1)}$ implies $A_b\le C^{\alpha/D}A_r$, proving the rate specialization. The conclusion has been proved using the corrected small-scale events and without the invalid all-scale premise or weight-comparability inference recorded in [F6].

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let all coefficients and data be real. Let $n\ge2$, and let $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and bounded with smooth boundary. Suppose $A,\beta,c,F,G$ are smooth on a neighborhood of $\bar V$, $A=A^T$, $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ for constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda$, and $c\le0$. For $L=A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+c$, the Dirichlet problem $Lu=F$ in $V$, $u=G$ on $\partial V$ has exactly one solution $u\in C^\infty(\bar V)$. Here smoothness on the closure means that all interior derivatives extend continuously to the closure, equivalently that a smooth extension exists to every finite differentiability order.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u$$
on $U$, where $a(x)$ is symmetric, $\xi^Ta(x)\xi\ge\lambda_0|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\lambda_0>0$, the coefficients are continuous and bounded, and $\widetilde c\le0$. There is a constant $C_L<\infty$, depending only on $U$, $\lambda_0$, and the coefficient bounds, such that every $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $L[w]\in C^0(U)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$
In particular, for any two functions $u^*,h\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$,
$$\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[u^*]-L[h]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. For finite real coefficient functions $a_{ij},b_i,c_i,d$ on $U$, the positive divergence-form expression is
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_iD_i u+du.$$
Its classical domain consists of those $u\in C^2(U)$ for which every displayed flux derivative $D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$ and $D_i(b_i u)$ exists pointwise and is finite on $U$. The classical formula assigns no value outside this domain. In particular, if each $D_i a_{ij}$ and $D_i b_i$ exists pointwise and is finite, the product rule makes every $u\in C^2(U)$ admissible and gives the nondivergence expansion
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
with
$$\widetilde b_j=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i a_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i b_i+d.$$
The **positive divergence convention** here means that the principal part is $+\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$. This sign is part of the definition.

When a weak formulation is used, its divergence derivatives are instead distributional derivatives of locally integrable fluxes, with the integrability hypotheses supplied in that formulation. Equality with a pointwise expression requires separate justification; pointwise differentiability alone does not assert it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
On every ball, $C^{2,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ therefore agrees with the finite-scaled-norm class of that dependency. This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

**Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice** ([[def-dependent-choice]]). Let
$(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space.

1. If $X$ is normal ([[def-normal-and-t4-spaces]]), $A \subseteq X$ is closed
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and $a \le b$ are reals, then every
   continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) extends to a continuous
   $F : X \to [a,b]$ with $F|_A = f$.
2. Conversely, if for every closed $A \subseteq X$ and every reals $a \le b$
   every continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ extends to a continuous $F : X \to [a,b]$
   with $F|_A = f$, then $X$ is normal. **This direction uses no choice
   principle.**

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1\le p<\infty$, and let
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ admit a representative
$\tilde u\in C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then, with $T$ the trace operator
of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]],
$$Tu=\tilde u|_{\partial\Omega}\qquad\text{in }L^p(\partial\Omega);$$
in particular $Tu=0$ whenever such a representative vanishes on
$\partial\Omega$. Two representatives continuous on $\overline\Omega$ of the
same class have the same restriction to $\partial\Omega$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$. For $u,v\ge0$,
$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $n\ge2$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Consider a family of bounded smooth domains $V$ in a fixed bounded set with a common finite boundary graph atlas: the graph radii, inverse-chart radii and bounds for all chart and inverse-chart derivatives through order two and the $\alpha$-Hölder seminorms of their second derivatives are uniformly controlled. Let $L=A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+c$ have real smooth coefficients near $\bar V$, with $A=A^T$, $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ for fixed $0<\lambda\le\Lambda$, and uniformly bounded global $C^{0,\alpha}(\bar V)$ coefficient norms. There is a uniform $C<\infty$ such that every real $u\in C^\infty(\bar V)$ with zero boundary values satisfies
$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar V)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;V}+\|Lu\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\bar V)}\bigr).$$
The constant depends only on the stated uniform geometric and coefficient controls, dimension and exponent, and not on higher smoothness norms. No sign of $c$ is required for this a priori estimate.

Furthermore every nonempty bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ has smooth bounded open subsets $V_j$ with $\bar V_j\subset U$, every compact subset of $U$ eventually contained in $V_j$, and a common finite graph atlas with the uniform controls just described. Nestedness is not asserted or required.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

derivations.claim: Expand the intended divergence expression by the product rule to obtain $L=A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+\gamma$. On a bounded Lipschitz domain, two sufficiently close points in a fixed smaller graph patch can be joined inside a larger patch by a path of length at most a fixed multiple of their distance; bounded first derivatives therefore give a Lipschitz bound for $a,b$ there. A finite cover and the supremum bound for separated pairs give their global Hölder bounds. Thus the finite global coefficient assumptions give finite Hölder bounds for the expanded coefficients, $\gamma\le0$, and a finite bound for $DA$. Throughout the proof write $c=\gamma$, and use $\lambda=\lambda_0$, $\Lambda=\Lambda_0$.

If $n=1$, the bounded Lipschitz set is a finite union of open intervals: its compact boundary has a finite one-sided graph-chart cover, and in dimension one each such chart contains one boundary point. On each interval $(a,b)$ all coefficients and $f$ extend Hölder-continuously to $[a,b]$ and $A\ge\lambda$. Write $y=(u,u')$, so $y'=M(x)y+F(x)$, where $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-c/A&-\beta/A\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $F=(0,f/A)$. For $Th(x)=\int_a^xM(t)h(t)\,dt$, iterated integration gives $\|T^kh\|_\infty\le \|h\|_\infty(\|M\|_\infty(b-a))^k/k!$. Therefore the uniformly convergent series $y=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k(y(a)+\int_a^{\cdot}F)$ solves the integral equation, hence the differential system; the factorial bound also proves uniqueness by iterating the homogeneous difference equation. Choose one particular solution with the prescribed left value and slope zero, and add $s$ times the homogeneous solution with initial value zero and slope one. That homogeneous solution cannot also vanish at $b$: otherwise [F2] would make it identically zero, contradicting its slope at $a$. Thus exactly one $s$ gives the prescribed right value. The equation makes $u''$ globally Hölder, so $u\in C^{2,\alpha}([a,b])$. Zero endpoint values imply $u\in H^1_0(a,b)$ directly: multiply by a cutoff vanishing within $\varepsilon$ of each endpoint, with derivative bounded by $C/\varepsilon$; since $|u|\le\|u'\|_\infty\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial(a,b))$, the cutoff error in $H^1$ tends to zero, and each compactly supported $H^1$ function is approximated by mollification. For zero data, integration against $u$ gives $\lambda\|u'\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2\|u\|_2+\|\beta-A'\|_\infty\|u'\|_2\|u\|_2+\|c\|_\infty\|u\|_2^2$; Young's inequality and [F2] then give the stated energy bound on these finitely many intervals. This proves all existence, energy, and global regularity conclusions in dimension one; [F2] gives stability. Henceforth take $n\ge2$.

Let $\delta(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus U)$ on all of $\mathbb R^n$; it is nonnegative, 1-Lipschitz, vanishes outside $U$, and has compact support because $U$ is bounded. Fix a nonnegative unit-mass smooth mollifier supported in the unit ball. Put $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$ and $\delta_j=\rho_{\varepsilon_j}*\delta$. Then $$|\delta_j-\delta|\le\varepsilon_j.$$ Choose a regular value $t_j\in(2\varepsilon_j,3\varepsilon_j)$, using the local Euclidean Morse–Sard theorem, and set $V_j=\{\delta_j>t_j\}$. This is bounded with compact smooth boundary, satisfies $\bar V_j\subset U$ (indeed $\delta\ge t_j-\varepsilon_j>\varepsilon_j$ on its closure), and contains $\{\delta>4\varepsilon_j\}$. Every compact subset of $U$ is contained in $V_j$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Discard an initial empty $V_j$ if necessary. Nestedness is not required anywhere below. If there are several components, use the same argument componentwise; a compact smooth boundary has a finite graph cover and the proof supplies the same finite-cover regularity on their union.

Choose $s_j<\varepsilon_j/4$ tending to zero and mollify the original coefficients and forcing at scale $s_j$ on a neighborhood of $\bar V_j$: $$A_j=\rho_{s_j}*A,\quad\beta_j=\rho_{s_j}*\beta,\quad c_j=\rho_{s_j}*c,\quad f_j=\rho_{s_j}*f.$$ Only values inside $U$ are used there. Consequently $A_j=A_j^T$, $\lambda I\le A_j\le\Lambda I$, $c_j\le0$, and the sup bounds of $\beta_j,c_j,f_j,DA_j$ do not exceed the original corresponding bounds. On every fixed interior ball, their Hölder norms are uniformly bounded and they converge uniformly to the original coefficients/data; $DA_j\to DA$ uniformly locally as well. The Hölder bound follows directly by integrating $|F(x-z)-F(y-z)|\le[F]_\alpha|x-y|^\alpha$. Each coefficient is smooth near $\bar V_j$; its higher derivatives can grow with $j$, which does not matter.

Extend $g$ to a bounded continuous $G$ on $\mathbb R^n$ using Tietze and set $G_j=\rho_{s_j}*G$. Uniform convergence $G_j\to G$ holds on any fixed compact neighborhood of $\bar U$, by uniform continuity there. Also $\|G_j\|_\infty\le\|G\|_\infty$. The lemma gives a smooth classical $u_j$ on $\bar V_j$ satisfying $$L_ju_j=f_j\quad\hbox{in }V_j,\qquad u_j=G_j\quad\hbox{on }\partial V_j.$$

Take a slab $a\le x_1\le b$ containing $\bar U$, put $B=\sup_j\|\beta_{j,1}\|_\infty$, $C_0=\sup_j\|c_j\|_\infty$, and choose $\kappa$ with $\lambda\kappa^2-B\kappa-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi=e^{\kappa x_1}$, $L_j\psi\ge e^{\kappa a}=:\eta>0$. Fix $M>e^{\kappa b}$ and put $\Phi=M-\psi>0$. Then $L_j\Phi\le-\eta$ for every $j$. The comparison implication used below follows directly: if $z\in C^2(V_j)\cap C(\bar V_j)$, $L_jz\ge0$ and $z\le0$ on $\partial V_j$, a value $z(x_0)>0$ would, for $\epsilon>0$ sufficiently small that $\epsilon e^{\kappa b}<z(x_0)$, force $z+\epsilon\psi$ to have a positive interior maximum. There its gradient is zero and Hessian negative semidefinite, so ellipticity and $c_j\le0$ give $L_j(z+\epsilon\psi)\le0$. This contradicts $L_j(z+\epsilon\psi)\ge\epsilon\eta>0$, proving $z\le0$.

Let $Q=\|G\|_\infty$ and $R=\|f\|_\infty$. On $\partial V_j$, both $u_j-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$ and $-u_j-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$ are nonpositive. Their $L_j$ images are nonnegative, since $c_j\le0$, $|f_j|\le R$ and $L_j\Phi\le-\eta$. Comparison gives $$|u_j|\le Q+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_\infty=:M_0$$ on $V_j$. This constant depends only on the original domain/slab, uniform ellipticity and expanded coefficient sup bounds, $R,Q$. It is independent of $j$, of the smoothness of $\partial V_j$, and of all higher coefficient derivatives.

For every ball $B_{2r}(x)\Subset U$, it is contained in $V_j$ for large $j$. Apply the actual interior Schauder theorem to $u_j$ there. All coefficient $C^\alpha$ norms and ellipticity constants are uniformly controlled on that fixed ball, $\|u_j\|_\infty\le M_0$, and the $C^\alpha$ norm of $f_j$ is uniformly bounded. Hence $u_j$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{2,\alpha}(B_r(x))$.

Cover $U$ by a countable family of such inner balls with rational centers/radii. Arzelà–Ascoli on each smaller closed ball and diagonal extraction give one subsequence for which $(u_j,Du_j,D^2u_j)$ converges uniformly on every compact subset of $U$. The fundamental theorem of calculus on coordinate segments identifies the limits with $(u,Du,D^2u)$; their compatibility on overlapping balls follows from uniform convergence. Passing each Hessian Hölder difference quotient to the limit proves $u\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Uniform local convergence of all coefficients/data and derivatives gives $Lu=f$ pointwise. The uniform bound gives $|u|\le M_0$.

Fix $q\in\partial U$. Let $B_R(z)$ be an exterior ball tangent at $q$. Replace it by the smaller ball with center $z'=(z+q)/2$ and radius $r_0=R/2$. Its **closed** ball is contained in $B_R(z)\cup\{q\}$: for $x\ne q$ on the smaller closed ball, strict triangle inequality gives $|x-z|<R$. Thus $$|x-z'|\ge r_0\quad(x\in\bar U),\qquad |x-z'|=r_0\iff x=q.$$ This strict contact property is necessary; the original exterior ball could touch the boundary at several points.

Write $r=|x-z'|$, $e=(x-z')/r$, and let $R_1=\max_{\bar U}r$. Choose an integer $m>0$ so large that $$(m+2)\lambda-n\Lambda-R_1\sup_j\|\beta_j\|_\infty\ge1.$$ Define $W_0=r_0^{-m}-r^{-m}$. It is smooth near $\bar U$, nonnegative there, vanishes exactly at $q$, and a direct differentiation gives $$L_jW_0=m r^{-m-2}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}A_j-(m+2)e^TA_je+r\beta_j\cdot e\bigr)+c_jW_0\le-mr^{-m-2}\le-mR_1^{-m-2}.$$ After multiplying by $R_1^{m+2}/m$, obtain a single $W_q\ge0$ with $W_q(q)=0$, $W_q>0$ on $\bar U\setminus\{q\}$, and $L_jW_q\le-1$ for every $j$.

Fix $0<\epsilon<1$. Continuity of $G$ at $q$ gives a neighborhood $N$ of $q$ where $|G(x)-g(q)|<\epsilon/2$. Uniform approximation gives $|G_j-G|<\epsilon/2$ on $\bar U$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Thus $|G_j-g(q)|<\epsilon$ on $N\cap\bar U$. On the compact complementary set $\bar U\setminus N$, $W_q$ has a strictly positive minimum; choose $K$ so large that $$|G_j-g(q)|\le\epsilon+KW_q\quad\hbox{on all of }\bar U$$ for all sufficiently large $j$, and also $$K\ge R+C_0(|g(q)|+\epsilon).$$ Apply comparison on $V_j$ to $$z_j^+=u_j-g(q)-\epsilon-KW_q,\qquad z_j^-=-u_j+g(q)-\epsilon-KW_q.$$ They are nonpositive on $\partial V_j$, and $$L_jz_j^+=f_j-c_j(g(q)+\epsilon)-KL_jW_q\ge-R-C_0(|g(q)|+\epsilon)+K\ge0,$$ $$L_jz_j^-=-f_j+c_j(g(q)-\epsilon)-KL_jW_q\ge-R-C_0(|g(q)|+\epsilon)+K\ge0.$$ Therefore $$|u_j(x)-g(q)|\le\epsilon+KW_q(x)\quad(x\in V_j)$$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Passing to the interior limit gives the same bound for $u$ on $U$. Let $x\to q$ from inside $U$ and use $W_q(x)\to0$; then $\limsup_{x\to q}|u(x)-g(q)|\le\epsilon$. Since $\epsilon$ was arbitrary, $u(x)\to g(q)$. Set $u=g$ on $\partial U$. The resulting function is continuous at every boundary point and in the interior, hence belongs to $C(\bar U)$.

This proves existence. The exponential-barrier comparison from the residual-stability lemma applied to the difference of two solutions proves uniqueness. Its stated residual estimate applied to $u-h$ proves the stability branch without any regularity of $h$ stronger than $C^2(U)\cap C(\bar U)$ plus bounded residual. No boundary-correction existence needs to be assumed.

Now set $g=0$ and choose $G=G_j=0$ exactly. Let $u_j$ be the corresponding approximants above. For them, the positive equation expands equivalently to $$\operatorname{div}(A_jDu_j)+q_j\cdot Du_j+c_ju_j=f_j,\qquad q_j=\beta_j-\operatorname{div}A_j.$$ The bounds on $DA_j,\beta_j$ give $\sup_j\|q_j\|_\infty\le Q_1<\infty$. This is where the original $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of $A$ is used; existence in the purely nondivergence formulation required only $C^\alpha$ principal coefficients after an appropriate different approximation argument.

Multiply by $u_j$, integrate over $V_j$, and use $u_j=0$ on its smooth boundary: $$\lambda\|Du_j\|_2^2\le\|f_j\|_2\|u_j\|_2+Q_1\|Du_j\|_2\|u_j\|_2+\|c_j\|_\infty\|u_j\|_2^2.$$ Young's inequality gives $$\|Du_j\|_2^2\le C\bigl(\|f_j\|_2^2+\|u_j\|_2^2\bigr).$$ The uniform supremum estimate with $Q=0$ yields $\|u_j\|_2\le |U|^{1/2}C\|f\|_\infty$, and $\|f_j\|_2\le|U|^{1/2}\|f\|_\infty$. Thus $$\sup_j\|u_j\|_{H^1(V_j)}\le C_U\|f\|_\infty.$$ Because $u_j$ is smooth to its smooth boundary and zero there, it lies in $H^1_0(V_j)$. Extend it by zero to $U$; approximation of each class by $C_c^\infty(V_j)\subset C_c^\infty(U)$ proves that this extension belongs to $H^1_0(U)$ and has the same $H^1$ norm.

For completeness, no unproved compactness premise is hidden here. In the Hilbert space $H^1_0(U)$, take the closed span of the countable sequence of extensions. Apply Gram–Schmidt to its listed vectors, discarding zeros, to obtain a finite or countable orthonormal basis of that span. Boundedness, diagonal extraction of the scalar coordinates, and Bessel's inequality give square-summable limiting coordinates and a vector in that closed span. Approximate each test vector by its finite basis sums; the common norm bound then proves convergence against every inner product test vector in that span. For any ambient Hilbert test vector $z$, finite Bessel bounds make the series of its coordinates in this basis converge in the closed span, and its residual is orthogonal to every basis vector and hence to the span; replacing $z$ by this series thus gives the same pairing; Riesz representation therefore proves weak convergence in the ambient Hilbert space, including convergence against the bounded $L^2$ pairings of functions and gradients. Its $L^2$ restriction to every compact interior ball agrees with $u$, since the chosen local-classical subsequence converges uniformly there. Thus the weak limit is the function $u$ almost everywhere on $U$. It follows that $$u\in H^1_0(U),\qquad\|u\|_{H^1(U)}\le C_U\|f\|_\infty.$$ Equivalently the weak limit in $H^1(U)$ remains in the closed linear subspace $H^1_0(U)$; the direct closed-span construction already takes place in that subspace.

Passing the original weak equations to the limit against any $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ is legitimate by local uniform convergence of coefficients/data and weak convergence of gradients. The divergence representation above shows that $u$ solves the variational equation; density extends it to all $H^1_0$ tests because $A,q,c,f$ are bounded. This establishes both the finite-energy membership and the correct weak interpretation, rather than inferring them from continuity and zero boundary values alone.

For a general $C^{2,\alpha}$ lifting $G$, apply this zero-boundary result to $v=u-G$ with forcing $f-LG\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$. Uniqueness of the classical Dirichlet problem identifies that zero-boundary solution with $u-G$.

Suppose $n\ge2$, $U$ is $C^{2,\alpha}$ and the datum has the stated ambient lifting $G$. Use the smooth interior approximating domains $V_j$ from [F8], which have uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ graph charts and eventually contain every compact subset of $U$. Write $d_j=\operatorname{dist}(\bar V_j,\mathbb R^n\setminus U)>0$. Repeat the already proved smooth-coefficient construction at scales $0<r_j<d_j/4$ tending to zero, so all coefficient, forcing and lifting convolution evaluations near $\bar V_j$ remain inside $U$. Uniform ellipticity, symmetry, the expanded-potential sign and all global $C^\alpha$ bounds are preserved. For the undifferentiated $a,b$ terms, their finite first-derivative bounds yield a global Lipschitz bound on this fixed smooth domain: in each graph patch, sufficiently close points are connected inside a slightly larger patch by a path of length at most $C|x-y|$; a finite cover handles close pairs and the supremum bound handles separated pairs. The prescribed highest-derivative Hölder norms then give the uniform expanded coefficient norms. The lifting mollifications have uniformly bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ norms and converge uniformly near the closure.

Let $u_j$ be the smooth Dirichlet solutions on $V_j$ with forcing $f_j$ and boundary lifting $G_j$. Their existence and smoothness up to the smooth boundary were proved by the Sobolev-bootstrap helper before using any boundary Schauder estimate. The exponential comparison gives a uniform supremum bound. Apply [F8] to the already smooth zero-boundary functions $w_j=u_j-G_j$, whose forcings $f_j-L_jG_j$ have uniformly bounded $C^\alpha$ norms. The domain geometry and coefficient controls are uniform, so $\sup_j\|u_j\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar V_j)}\le C(\|f\|_{0,\alpha;U}+\|G\|_{2,\alpha;\bar U})$.

The existing interior compactness and exterior-ball boundary comparison arguments give a subsequence converging locally in $C^2(U)$ to the unique classical Dirichlet solution $u$. The displayed global derivative bounds pass to this local limit. For any fixed distinct $x,y\in U$, both points eventually lie in $V_j$, so their second-derivative Hölder quotient passes to the limit with the same common bound. Hence $D^2u$ is bounded and globally $\alpha$-Hölder on $U$, and extends continuously to the closure. The function and gradient extend continuously as well: bounded first and second derivatives give Lipschitz bounds along the controlled-length local interior paths in each graph patch, and separated pairs are bounded by the global suprema. These extensions are the continuous extensions of the interior derivatives. Consequently $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar U)$ with the stated data estimate, obtained entirely from smooth approximants without assuming the original solution's boundary Hölder norm. Together with the parent's one-dimensional argument and the prior local existence, uniqueness, stability and energy steps, all branches follow.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let all coefficients and data be real. Let $n\ge1$, $0<\alpha<1$, and let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, bounded and Lipschitz, with an exterior ball at every boundary point. Suppose $a_{ij}=a_{ji},b_i\in C^{1,\alpha}(U)$ and $c_i,d\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$, with finite global norms, and $\lambda_0 I\le A=(a_{ij})\le\Lambda_0 I$ for constants $0<\lambda_0\le\Lambda_0$. Define
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_ju)+\sum_iD_i(b_i u)+\sum_i c_iD_iu+du,$$
$$\beta_j=\sum_iD_ia_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \gamma=\sum_iD_ib_i+d,$$
and assume $\gamma\le0$. Retain, when required by the source application, the bounds $\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2\le\Lambda$ and $\lambda_0^{-2}(|b|^2+|c|^2)+\lambda_0^{-1}|d|\le v^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

citations.quote:
Fix an input dimension $q\ge1$ and an integer $m\ge0$. Let $\mathcal A_m^{(q)}$ be the class of continuous scalar activations $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ for which there is one depth $n\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, the scalar-output depth-$n$ multilayer perceptrons with activation $\sigma$ are dense in $C^m(K)$ in the $C^m$ norm. For $m=0$, $C^0(K)$ has the supremum norm. For $m>0$, $C^m(K)$ means jets of functions defined and $C^m$ on an open neighborhood of $K$: identify two functions when all their derivatives of orders at most $m$ agree on $K$, and use the norm $\max_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|D^\beta f(x)|$. Only networks that are $C^m$ near $K$ enter this density assertion. For vector outputs, stack scalar-output networks of that same depth. The source notation $\mathcal A_m$ suppresses the input dimension fixed by the finite-dimensional network under consideration. Let $\mathcal A_m^{L,(q)}$ be the subclass whose members are Borel measurable and have at most linear growth, meaning
$$\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\frac{|\sigma(s)|}{1+|s|}<\infty.$$
For an integer $q\ge1$, define $\mathrm{BA}_q$ to consist of those $\sigma\in\mathcal A_0^{(q)}$ for which, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $\varepsilon>0$, and every $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$, there is a finite multilayer perceptron $f:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q$ with
$$|f(x)-x|_2\le\varepsilon\quad(x\in K),\qquad |f(x)|_2\le C\quad(x\in\mathbb R^q).$$
Here $\operatorname{diam}_2(K)=\sup_{x,y\in K}|x-y|_2$, with diameter and all displayed approximation seminorms equal to zero on the empty set. The diameter-based global bound is part of this definition and is retained verbatim; whether it has any members is checked separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz open set, with $d\ge1$, and let $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $X$ be either $W^{m,p}(D;\mathbb R)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, including $W^{0,p}(D)=L^p(D)$, or $C^m(\bar D;\mathbb R)$. In the latter space derivatives in $D$ extend continuously to $\bar D$, and the norm is $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha u|$. For every norm-compact $K\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank linear map $F:X\to X$ such that $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$ and whose range is contained in the restrictions to $D$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, with their continuous boundary values in the $C^m$ case. In particular, such smooth restrictions are norm-dense in $X$.

Moreover, there are finitely many ambient smooth cutoffs $\psi_j$, vectors $v_j$, a unit-mass $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, and $t_0>0$ such that for $0<t<t_0$ the kernel $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, with $\rho_t(z)=t^{-d}\rho(z/t)$, defines bounded linear smoothing maps $S_tu(x)=\int_Dk_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. They satisfy $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}<\infty$ and $\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|_X\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Each kernel is ambient smooth with fixed compact support in its first variable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge1$ and use the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family

$$\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}=\left\{x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j):m\in\mathbb N_0,\ c,a_j,b_j\in\mathbb R,\ w_j\in\mathbb R^d\right\}.$$

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. More generally, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is not polynomial almost everywhere, this family is dense for the essential-supremum seminorm on each such $K$ with respect to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. If instead $\sigma$ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial of degree at most $q$ for some $q\in\mathbb N_0$ (including the zero polynomial), the family is not uniformly dense on the segment $\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}$, and is not dense in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm on $[0,1]^d$. Thus pointwise compact-uniform density for $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, and essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$, each hold on every compact set if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere.

Let $1<p<\infty$, and let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, a network is interpreted in this space through any Borel representative agreeing with it outside a Lebesgue-null set; these representatives exist, are integrable on $K$, and give a unique $L^p(\mu)$ class. This convention does not alter the actual pointwise network used in the uniform clause. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)>0$, $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If $\mu=0$, then $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)=\{0\}$ and the network family is dense for every $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, including polynomial activations.

These are existence statements without a quantitative width bound. They imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization, and compact-uniform approximation does not mean uniform approximation on all of $\mathbb R^d$.
For each $q\ge1$, the class $\mathrm{BA}_q$ in the displayed activation-class definition is empty.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

Thus each smooth moment $a\mapsto\int_D\varphi a$ is continuous on $A$ and such moments separate distinct members of $K$, using [F4]; distinct continuous functions also differ on an interior set of positive measure.

ReLU is continuous and Borel, is pointwise bounded on every compact interval, and has empty discontinuity set, so it belongs to $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$. It cannot agree almost everywhere with a polynomial: that polynomial would vanish on the negative half-line by continuity, hence identically, contradicting ReLU on the positive half-line. Composition of layered MLPs is a layered MLP because consecutive affine maps merge. ReLU also has linear growth and belongs to every relevant $\mathcal A_0$ by [F6]. Thus this corrected branch is nonvacuous.

The set $Q=\{(a,b)\in K^2:\|T(a)-T(b)\|_U\ge\tau\}$ is compact. For each pair in $Q$ a separating moment from step 1.1 remains nonzero on a neighborhood of that pair.
