citations.quote: For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

The raw quadrature rule below takes the continuous input function, including any off-grid values used by a local term or pointwise lifting. It is not by itself asserted to factor through its stored input samples. A finite-sampling version is specified after the raw rule.

For the continuous-function architecture, take its pointwise lift $P$, layers indexed by $0\le t<L$, and pointwise projection $Q$. Given a finite partition of $D$ into nonempty measurable cells $E_1,\dots,E_N$, choose tags $\xi_j\in E_j$ and weights $\omega_j=|E_j|$. Initialize the raw lifted field $v_{0,n}(x)=P(a(x))$ on $\bar D$ and store $v_{0,n}(\xi_j)$. For each layer whose output domain is $\bar D$, define at every $x\in\bar D$
$$v_{t+1,n}(x)=\sigma_t\!\left(W_tv_{t,n}(x)+\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\kappa_t(x,\xi_j)v_{t,n}(\xi_j)+b_t(x)\right),$$
and store its values at all tags for the next layer. If the last layer instead has output domain $\bar D'\ne\bar D$, use its required zero local term and define, for $x\in\bar D'$,
$$v_{L,n}(x)=\sigma_{L-1}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\kappa_{L-1}(x,\xi_j)v_{L-1,n}(\xi_j)+b_{L-1}(x)\right).$$
Return the function $x\mapsto Q(v_{L,n}(x))$ on the output closure, evaluating these same formulas at each requested query point. A refinement changes cells, tags, and weights, while all layer, lifting, and projection parameters remain fixed.

For a finite-sampling realization on continuous inputs, first reconstruct the input from its prescribed tags by the normalized nonnegative weights in the finite-sampling reconstruction bridge. Run the raw rule on this reconstructed function, including in the pointwise lifting and every local term. Its output is then a function of the finite input sample vector alone, with the same continuum parameters. The weights and reconstruction change with the partition; the learned parameters do not. Along partition sequences whose maximal cell diameters $h_n=\max_j\operatorname{diam}(E_{n,j})$ tend to zero, if the raw maps converge compact-uniformly in the output supremum norm, the bridge transfers that convergence to this finite-sampling realization. For a stronger compatible Banach input/output formulation, supply reconstructions into the actual input Banach space that converge compact-uniformly in that input norm; the same bridge then preserves the raw rule's proved output Banach norm convergence. The explicit continuous-input weights alone do not assert this stronger reconstruction property.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge1$ and use the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family

$$\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}=\left\{x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j):m\in\mathbb N_0,\ c,a_j,b_j\in\mathbb R,\ w_j\in\mathbb R^d\right\}.$$

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. More generally, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is not polynomial almost everywhere, this family is dense for the essential-supremum seminorm on each such $K$ with respect to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. If instead $\sigma$ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial of degree at most $q$ for some $q\in\mathbb N_0$ (including the zero polynomial), the family is not uniformly dense on the segment $\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}$, and is not dense in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm on $[0,1]^d$. Thus pointwise compact-uniform density for $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, and essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$, each hold on every compact set if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere.

Let $1<p<\infty$, and let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, a network is interpreted in this space through any Borel representative agreeing with it outside a Lebesgue-null set; these representatives exist, are integrable on $K$, and give a unique $L^p(\mu)$ class. This convention does not alter the actual pointwise network used in the uniform clause. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)>0$, $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If $\mu=0$, then $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)=\{0\}$ and the network family is dense for every $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, including polynomial activations.

These are existence statements without a quantitative width bound. They imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization, and compact-uniform approximation does not mean uniform approximation on all of $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

Fix an input dimension $q\ge1$ and an integer $m\ge0$. Let $\mathcal A_m^{(q)}$ be the class of continuous scalar activations $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ for which there is one depth $n\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, the scalar-output depth-$n$ multilayer perceptrons with activation $\sigma$ are dense in $C^m(K)$ in the $C^m$ norm. For $m=0$, $C^0(K)$ has the supremum norm. For $m>0$, $C^m(K)$ means jets of functions defined and $C^m$ on an open neighborhood of $K$: identify two functions when all their derivatives of orders at most $m$ agree on $K$, and use the norm $\max_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|D^\beta f(x)|$. Only networks that are $C^m$ near $K$ enter this density assertion. For vector outputs, stack scalar-output networks of that same depth. The source notation $\mathcal A_m$ suppresses the input dimension fixed by the finite-dimensional network under consideration. Let $\mathcal A_m^{L,(q)}$ be the subclass whose members are Borel measurable and have at most linear growth, meaning
$$\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\frac{|\sigma(s)|}{1+|s|}<\infty.$$
For an integer $q\ge1$, define $\mathrm{BA}_q$ to consist of those $\sigma\in\mathcal A_0^{(q)}$ for which, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $\varepsilon>0$, and every $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$, there is a finite multilayer perceptron $f:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q$ with
$$|f(x)-x|_2\le\varepsilon\quad(x\in K),\qquad |f(x)|_2\le C\quad(x\in\mathbb R^q).$$
Here $\operatorname{diam}_2(K)=\sup_{x,y\in K}|x-y|_2$, with diameter and all displayed approximation seminorms equal to zero on the empty set. The diameter-based global bound is part of this definition and is retained verbatim; whether it has any members is checked separately.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For integers $n\ge2$ put $t_n=3\cdot2^{-n-2}$, $w_n=2^{-4n-4}$, $H_n=2^{2n}$ and $\rho_n(s)=H_n\beta((s-t_n)/w_n)$. Their supports are disjoint subintervals of $(0,1)$: successive centers differ by $3\cdot2^{-n-3}$, which exceeds $w_n+w_{n+1}$, and each radius is smaller than its center. Define $\rho(s)=\sum_{n\ge2}\rho_n(s)$ for $s>0$, and $\rho(s)=0$ for $s\le0$. On each compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$ only finitely many summands are nonzero. Moreover $m_n=\int\rho_n\le2H_nw_n=2^{-2n-3}$, so $B=\sum_{n\ge2}m_n<1$. Define $\sigma(s)=\int_0^s\rho(t)\,dt$ for $s\ge0$ and $\sigma(s)=0$ for $s<0$. The tail mass bound proves continuity at zero and uniform convergence of the primitives $\sigma_n(s)=\int_0^s\rho_n(t)\,dt$; thus $\sigma=\sum\sigma_n$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, bounded by $B$, and smooth on $(0,\infty)$. It is a legitimate continuous activation. It is bounded and nonconstant, hence is not polynomial even almost everywhere: continuity would make an almost-everywhere polynomial identity hold everywhere, and a bounded polynomial is constant. Both $\sigma$ and ReLU are continuous, hence Borel measurable with empty discontinuity set, and pointwise bounded on every compact interval (globally for $\sigma$, and by the interval radius for ReLU). They therefore belong to $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ in [F3]. ReLU is not polynomial almost everywhere: continuity would give a polynomial identity everywhere, while vanishing on the negative half-line forces that polynomial to be zero, contradicting its positive values. Applying [F3] in each input dimension now places $\sigma$ in every $\mathcal A_0$ class and ReLU in every $\mathcal A_0^L$ class; ReLU is Borel and obeys $|\operatorname{ReLU}(s)|\le|s|$.

Set $\kappa(x,y)=\sigma(x+y)$ and $G(a)(x)=\int_0^1\sigma(x+y)a(y)\,dy$. The kernel is exactly a one-hidden-unit network on $(x,y)$ with weights $(1,1)$, activation $\sigma$, output weight $1$, and zero biases. The other activations can be the identity. Each $G_n^*(a)(x)=\int_0^1\sigma_n(x+y)a(y)\,dy$ is $C^1$, with derivative $\int_0^1\rho_n(x+y)a(y)\,dy$, and both its function norm and derivative norm are at most $m_n\|a\|_\infty$. Consequently both the function series and derivative series converge uniformly. To verify differentiation without an interchange assumption, the finite partial sums satisfy $S_N(x)-S_N(0)=\int_0^x S_N'(t)\,dt$; uniform convergence permits passage to the limit in this equality, and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives a continuous derivative. Hence $G:A\to U$ is bounded linear, with $\|G(a)\|_U\le2B\|a\|_\infty$. Both $A$ and $U$ embed continuously into $C([0,1])$. To instantiate the source integral subclass as well, take $S_0$ and $S_1$ to have constant kernel $1$ and zero bias, and use $\kappa(x,y)=\sigma(x+y)$ as the final kernel, choosing ReLU for the input and intermediate kernel networks and activations. No intermediate activation occurs at depth $N=2$. This yields $\widehat G(a)=(\int_0^1a)G(1)$, a bounded map $A\to U$. For $a=1$, both preceding integral layers and their quadratures are exactly the constant $1$, so its final continuum and quadrature outputs are precisely those analyzed below. Constant kernels are exact networks through their affine output biases.

At refinement $n$ partition $(0,1)$ into $2^n$ dyadic cells of length $h_n=2^{-n}$. Choose the first tag to be $t_n\in(0,h_n)$ and choose the midpoint of every other cell. Let $Q_n(a)(x)=h_n\sum_{j=1}^{2^n}\sigma(x+\xi_{n,j})a(\xi_{n,j})$. These are compatible tagged Riemann sums, with mesh diameter tending to zero and the same continuum parameters at every refinement. Since every tag is positive, each summand is smooth in a neighborhood of $[0,1]$, so $Q_n(a)\in U$. For $a=1$, all derivative summands are nonnegative and $Q_n(1)'(0)\ge h_n\rho(t_n)=h_nH_n=2^n$. On the other hand, substitution in the continuum integral gives $G(1)(x)=\int_x^{x+1}\sigma(s)\,ds$ and $G(1)'(0)=\sigma(1)-\sigma(0)=B$. Thus $\|Q_n(1)-G(1)\|_U\ge2^n-B\to\infty$.

The set $K=\{1\}\subset A$ is compact. The continuous integrand $(x,y)\mapsto\sigma(x+y)$ on $[0,1]^2$ is uniformly continuous: otherwise pairs at distances tending to zero with a fixed positive function gap have convergent subsequences in the compact square and contradict continuity. Writing its modulus of continuity as $\omega$, the cellwise estimate gives $\|Q_n(1)-G(1)\|_\infty\le\omega(h_n)\to0$. Thus the genuine supremum-norm conclusion coexists with divergence in the admissible output norm, refuting the asserted inference.

Let $X$ be a Banach space. It has the **approximation property** (AP) if for
every norm-compact set $C\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a
bounded finite-rank operator $T:X\to X$ such that

$$\sup_{x\in C}\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon.$$

Here finite rank means that $T(X)$ is finite-dimensional.

For $\lambda\ge0$, $X$ has the **$\lambda$-bounded approximation property**
($\lambda$-BAP) if the same assertion holds with the additional operator-norm
bound $\|T\|\le\lambda$, where the norm is that of [[def-operator-norm]]. It
has the **bounded approximation property** (BAP) if it has $\lambda$-BAP for
some finite $\lambda$.

No sequence of approximating operators is required; this matters in
nonseparable spaces. Plainly $\lambda$-BAP implies AP.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K \in \{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and the complex case by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. Let
$e:n\to X$ be an ordered basis ([[def-linear-basis]]), and write $e_j:=e(j)$.
Give $\mathbb K^n$ its coordinate $\ell^1$ norm

$$\|(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})\|_1:=\sum_{j<n}|a_j|.$$

Define

$$T:\mathbb K^n\to X,\qquad T(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})=\sum_{j<n} a_j e_j.$$

Then $T$ is a topological isomorphism of normed spaces in the sense of
[[def-topological-isomorphism-of-normed-spaces]].

derivations.claim: If $K$ is empty use zero maps. Otherwise consider all pairs $(x,\rho)$ with $x\in K$ and $\rho>0$ such that $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/4$ whenever $\|z-x\|_X<3\rho$. Continuity ensures that the balls $B(x,\rho)$ from this family cover $K$; take a finite subcover $B(x_i,\rho_i)$. Put $\delta=\min_i\rho_i>0$. For $x\in K$ and $z\in X$ with $\|z-x\|_X<\delta$, select $i$ with $\|x-x_i\|_X<\rho_i$; then both $x,z$ lie within $3\rho_i$ of $x_i$, so $\|T(z)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. No compact neighborhood of $K$ is asserted or needed.

Apply AP in $X$ to choose bounded finite-rank $P$ with $\sup_K\|Px-x\|_X<\delta$. By step 1.1, $\sup_K\|T(Px)-T(x)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. The set $T(P(K))$ is compact; apply AP in $Y$ to obtain bounded finite-rank $Q$ with $\sup_{x\in K}\|QT(Px)-T(Px)\|_Y<\varepsilon/2$. Thus $QT P$ approximates $T$ on $K$ within $\varepsilon$. This makes only two AP selections and does not require a sequence, an infinite union of compact sets, or a choice principle for sequences.

Choose a finite basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_J$ of $P(X)$. Its coordinate functionals are bounded by [F2]; hence $Px=\sum_j\ell_j(x)\alpha_j$ with $\ell_j$ bounded on $X$, by composing those functionals with $P$. Write $Rz=\sum_jz_j\alpha_j$, $E(x)=(\ell_j(x))_j$. Choose a finite basis $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_s$ of $Q(Y)$, with bounded coordinate functionals $c_i$, and put $h_i(z)=c_i(QT(Rz))$ and $Bv=\sum_i v_i\beta_i$. Each $h_i$ is continuous on all $\mathbb R^J$, and $BhE=QTP$. For a zero-dimensional range use one zero basis vector and the zero coefficient map instead of an actual basis. These formulas prove the stated factorization and complete the proof.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice for the weak-derivative uniqueness interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$1\le p\le\infty$. For either real or complex scalars, the displayed
$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ formula from
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] is independent of the representatives
of its Sobolev and derivative classes and defines a norm: it is finite,
absolutely homogeneous, subadditive, and zero exactly on the zero $L^p$ class.
This holds at $p=1$ and $p=\infty$, and when $k=0$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the only class is zero and the formula is zero.

Under the page measure convention, if a finite family of open sets $U_j\subset\mathbb R^n$ covers compact K, there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ such that $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighborhood of K. These are ambient smooth functions, also when K is only a $C^1$ hypersurface.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Assume countable choice, let $n\ge1$, and use Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Translation $\tau_hf(x)=f(x-h)$ is an isometry of complex $L^p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$ and depends norm-continuously on $h$ for $p<\infty$.

For complex $K\in L^1$ and $f\in L^p$, the convolution
$$(K*f)(x)=\int K(y)f(x-y)\,dy$$
exists absolutely a.e., defines a measurable class independent of representatives, and satisfies $\|K*f\|_p\le\|K\|_1\|f\|_p$.

If $K_\varepsilon\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ satisfy
$$\int K_\varepsilon=1,\qquad M:=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty,\qquad \int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy\longrightarrow0\quad(\delta>0),$$
then $K_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$ for $p<\infty$, and uniformly for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. For fixed $K\in L^1$, $K*f\in C_0$ when $f\in C_0$. These assertions allow complex and sign-changing kernels. In particular $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}K(x/\varepsilon)$ is such an approximate identity whenever $K\in L^1$ and $\int K=1$.

If $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ has mass one, $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and $f$ is complex locally integrable, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f)=(\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon)*f.$$
A compactly supported input gives a compactly supported output. No general $L^\infty$ translation-continuity or approximate-identity convergence is asserted.

Let $(X,\mu)$ and $(Y,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces, let
$1 \le p < \infty$, and let $F : X \times Y \to \mathbb{C}$ be measurable with

$$ \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y) < \infty. $$

Then the function
$$ H(x) := \int_Y |F(x,y)|\,d\nu(y) $$
belongs to $L^p(X)$ and

$$ \|H\|_{L^p(X)} \le \int_Y \|F(\cdot,y)\|_{L^p(X)}\,d\nu(y). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: If $D=\varnothing$, $X$ is the zero space; take $F=0$, the empty cutoff family, $k_t=0$, $S_t=0$ and $t_0=1$. If $K=\varnothing$ the compact approximation clause is vacuous and $F=0$ suffices; the smoothing construction below depends only on $D$ and $X$, and can be obtained by carrying it out with $K=\{0\}$. Henceforth both sets are nonempty. In particular $0<|D|<\infty$, because $D$ contains a ball and is bounded. Fix one boundary chart $Q$, with Lipschitz graph function $\varphi$ of constant $L$, and an ambient neighborhood $U$ of its boundary point with $\bar U\subset Q$ compact. In chart coordinates set $v=(L+2)e_d$. For $x\in\bar D\cap\bar U$, $|z|\le1$, and sufficiently small $t>0$, uniformly in $x,z$, the point $y=x+tv-tz$ stays in $Q$ because $t(|v|+1)<\operatorname{dist}(\bar U,Q^c)$. Moreover $y_d-\varphi(y')\ge x_d-\varphi(x')+t(L+2)-t|z_d|-Lt|z'|\ge t>0$. Thus $\overline B(x+tv,t)\Subset D$. Rotate $v$ back to the original coordinates.

The compact boundary admits finitely many such $U_j$, $1\le j\le J$, covering it. The compact remainder $\bar D\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^JU_j$ lies in $D$; cover it by finitely many balls with closures in $D$, and let $U_0$ be their union, omitting it if the remainder is empty. Then $\bar U_0\Subset D$, so $v_0=0$ has the same ball property for sufficiently small $t$. Apply [F2] to this finite open cover of $\bar D$, obtaining $\psi_j\in C_c^\infty(U_j)$ with $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$. The minimum of the finitely many positive bounds on $t$ gives $t_0>0$ such that $\overline B(x+tv_j,t)\Subset D$ for every $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$ and $0<t<t_0$. Taking the family of all admissible chart neighborhoods before extracting a finite subcover avoids selecting a chart independently at every boundary point.

By [F9] choose a nonnegative smooth bump compactly supported in $B_1(0)$ and positive on $\overline B_{1/2}(0)$, and divide it by its positive integral to obtain $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B_1(0))$ with $\int\rho=1$. Put $\rho_t(w)=t^{-d}\rho(w/t)$. Every $u\in X$ belongs continuously to $L^1(D)$: use [F8] for Sobolev spaces, and $\|u\|_1\le |D|\|u\|_{C^m}$ for $C^m$. For its zero extension $E_0u$ define $H_{j,t}u(x)=(\rho_t*E_0u)(x+tv_j)$ and $S_tu=\sum_j\psi_jH_{j,t}u$. By [F4] these are well-defined linear constructions independent of representatives and $S_tu\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$.

First take $X=W^{m,p}(D)$. For every $|\gamma|\le m$ and $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, [F3] and step 2.1 give $$D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)=\int\rho(z)(E_0D^\gamma u)(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz.$$ The translated center has distance greater than $t$ from $D^c$: the entire closed ball of radius $t$ is a compact subset of $D$. The identity consequently holds on a neighborhood of each indicated $x$. Equivalently the defining weak-derivative identity can be tested against $y\mapsto\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, whose support is compact in $D$; its two derivative signs cancel. Only interior values are used, with no assertion that derivatives commute with zero extension across $\partial D$.

For $f\in L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ define $T_{j,t}f(x)=\int\rho(z)f(x+t(v_j-z))\,dz$ and $\omega_f(r)=\sup_{|h|\le r}\|f(\cdot+h)-f\|_p$. Translation invariance and [F5] give $\|T_{j,t}f\|_p\le\|f\|_p$ and $$\|T_{j,t}f-f\|_p\le\omega_f((|v_j|+1)t).$$ By [F4], $\omega_f(r)\to0$ as $r\downarrow0$. The integral estimates also apply when $p=1$, where [F5] follows directly from Tonelli.

Fix $0<t<t_0$. Write $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, so $S_tu(x)=\int_D k_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. Fix a closed box $Q$ containing $\bar D$. The finitely many $D_x^\alpha k_t$, $|\alpha|\le m$, are smooth and uniformly continuous on the compact set $\bar D\times Q$ by [F7]. For any $\eta>0$, partition $Q$ into finitely many measurable cells $Q_\ell$ of small enough diameter, assigning shared and outer faces consistently, and choose $y_\ell\in Q_\ell$. Their diameters can be chosen so that $|D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y)-D_x^\alpha k_t(x,y_\ell)|<\eta$ for $x\in\bar D$, $y\in Q_\ell$ and $|\alpha|\le m$. The point $y_\ell$ need not lie in $D$.

Set $f_\gamma=E_0D^\gamma u$. The finite Leibniz rule [F6], step 4.1 and $\sum_j\psi_j=1$ near $\bar D$ give, for $|\alpha|\le m$, the a.e. identity on $D$ $$D^\alpha(S_tu-u)=\sum_j\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\psi_j)\bigl(T_{j,t}f_{\alpha-\beta}-D^{\alpha-\beta}u\bigr).$$ Every derivative $D^\beta\psi_j$ vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, so step 4.1 supplies exactly the identities used in this formula. All these fixed multiplier derivatives are bounded. Step 4.2 and the finite norm sum [F1] therefore imply $\|S_tu-u\|_{W^{m,p}}\to0$. The same Leibniz formula without subtracting $u$, and $\|T_{j,t}f_\gamma\|_p\le\|f_\gamma\|_p\le\|u\|_{W^{m,p}}$, give $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$. For example take the $\ell^p$ norm over $\alpha$ of $\sum_{j,\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}\|D^\beta\psi_j\|_\infty$. This argument includes $m=0$ and $p=1$.

Now take $X=C^m(\bar D)$. By [F6] each bounded classical derivative is its weak derivative, so $u\in W^{m,1}(D)$ and step 4.1 applies. Each $D^\gamma u$ is uniformly continuous on $\bar D$ by [F7]. For $x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j$, every sampled $y=x+t(v_j-z)$ lies in $D$ and $|y-x|\le(|v_j|+1)t$. Positivity and mass one of $\rho$ thus give $$\sup_{x\in\bar D\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi_j}|D^\gamma H_{j,t}u(x)-D^\gamma u(x)|\le\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\bar D\\|x-y|\le(|v_j|+1)t}}|D^\gamma u(y)-D^\gamma u(x)|\longrightarrow0.$$ The formula of step 5.1, first on $D$ and then by continuity on $\bar D$, gives $\|S_tu-u\|_{C^m}\to0$. Bounding each averaged derivative by $\|D^\gamma u\|_\infty$ and summing the same fixed multiplier constants gives $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}\le M_X<\infty$ also in this case.

Define $$F_{t,\eta}u(x)=\sum_\ell k_t(x,y_\ell)\int_{D\cap Q_\ell}u(y)\,dy.$$ Each coefficient is a bounded linear functional by step 3.1, and there are finitely many coefficients. Each range function $k_t(\cdot,y_\ell)$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, so the operator has finite rank with the required smooth range. Comparison with the integral for $S_t$ gives $$\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha(F_{t,\eta}-S_t)u|\le\eta\|u\|_{L^1(D)}.$$ For $X=C^m(\bar D)$, this yields $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le |D|\eta$. For $X=W^{m,p}(D)$ let $A_m$ be the finite number of multi-indices of order at most $m$. Taking the derivative $L^p$ norms and then applying [F8] gives $\|F_{t,\eta}-S_t\|_{X\to X}\le A_m^{1/p}|D|^{1/p}\eta |D|^{1-1/p}=A_m^{1/p}|D|\eta$. This includes $p=1$, and it shows each $F_{t,\eta}$ is bounded because $S_t$ is bounded.

By steps 5.1 and 6.1 the operators $S_t:X\to X$ converge pointwise to the identity and satisfy $\|S_t\|\le M_X$. Choose $\delta<\varepsilon/[4(M_X+1)]$. Compactness gives a finite $\delta$-net $u_1,\ldots,u_N$ in $K$. Pointwise convergence permits one $t\in(0,t_0)$ such that $\max_i\|S_tu_i-u_i\|<\varepsilon/4$. For any $u\in K$, choose one net point within $\delta$; then $\|S_tu-u\|\le(M_X+1)\delta+\max_i\|S_tu_i-u_i\|<\varepsilon/2$. Compactness also makes $R=\sup_{u\in K}\|u\|$ finite: a finite cover by unit balls bounds all these norms by one plus the largest center norm.

Choose $\eta>0$ small enough that the relevant bound in step 7.1 is below $\varepsilon/[2(R+1)]$. For $F=F_{t,\eta}$, $$\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|\le\|F-S_t\|R+\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|<\varepsilon.$$ Its range is a finite span of ambient compactly supported smooth functions by step 7.1. Applying this conclusion to the singleton compact set $K=\{u\}$ proves smooth-restriction density for every $u\in X$. All net, partition and representative-point choices here are finite; Countable Choice enters only the analytical interfaces stated above.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz open set, with $d\ge1$, and let $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $X$ be either $W^{m,p}(D;\mathbb R)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, including $W^{0,p}(D)=L^p(D)$, or $C^m(\bar D;\mathbb R)$. In the latter space derivatives in $D$ extend continuously to $\bar D$, and the norm is $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha u|$. For every norm-compact $K\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank linear map $F:X\to X$ such that $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$ and whose range is contained in the restrictions to $D$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, with their continuous boundary values in the $C^m$ case. In particular, such smooth restrictions are norm-dense in $X$.

Moreover, there are finitely many ambient smooth cutoffs $\psi_j$, vectors $v_j$, a unit-mass $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, and $t_0>0$ such that for $0<t<t_0$ the kernel $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, with $\rho_t(z)=t^{-d}\rho(z/t)$, defines bounded linear smoothing maps $S_tu(x)=\int_Dk_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. They satisfy $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}<\infty$ and $\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|_X\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Each kernel is ambient smooth with fixed compact support in its first variable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Under the page measure convention, if a finite family of open sets $U_j\subset\mathbb R^n$ covers compact K, there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ such that $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighborhood of K. These are ambient smooth functions, also when K is only a $C^1$ hypersurface.

derivations.claim: Empty $K$ or $L=0$ is handled by $\kappa=0$. Otherwise [F1] permits choosing $t>0$ with $\sup_K\|S_ta-a\|_X<\varepsilon/(2\|L\|)$. For fixed $t$, the map $y\mapsto k_t(\cdot,y)|_D$ is ambient $C^\infty$ with values in $X$: every mixed $x$ and $y$ derivative is uniformly continuous on compact products, so the ordinary finite-dimensional Taylor remainders in $y$, uniformly for $x$ derivatives through order $m$, tend to zero in the $C^m$ norm and hence in the $X$ norm. Thus $\kappa_t(y)=L(k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$ is ambient smooth, with $D_y^\alpha\kappa_t=L(D_y^\alpha k_t(\cdot,y)|_D)$. It is bounded on $\bar D$.

Compactness of $K$ in $X$ implies its compactness in $L^1(D)$ by [F2]. Given $\theta>0$, take a finite $\theta/2$ net $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ in that $L^1$ image. By integrability and an exhaustion of $D$ by compact subsets, there is one compact $F\subset D$ with $\int_{D\setminus F}|a_i|<\theta/2$ for all $i$. Therefore $\sup_{a\in K}\int_{D\setminus F}|a|<\theta$. Choose a smooth cutoff $0\le\zeta\le1$, compactly supported in $D$, equal to one on $F$; use [F3] for the one-set open cover $\{D\}$ of $F$. Then $\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\theta$. This uses a finite net and finitely many integrable tails, including at $p=1$; it requires no $L^\infty$ approximation of a dual coefficient.

For each $a\in X$, one has $L(S_ta)=\int_D\kappa_t(y)a(y)\,dy$. To justify the identity without assuming a vector-integration theorem, partition a box containing $D$ into cells of diameter tending to zero and replace $k_t(\cdot,y)$ on each cell by $k_t(\cdot,y_l)$. Uniform continuity of every $x$ derivative through order $m$ makes the error in $X$ at most $c_X\eta\|a\|_1$, where $\eta\to0$ is the uniform kernel derivative error and $c_X$ converts a $C^m$ bound to an $X$ bound. Applying bounded $L$ to the finite sums is legitimate by linearity. Their scalar integral errors are at most $\|L\|c_X\eta\|a\|_1$ as well, so passing to the limit proves the identity. Consequently $\sup_K|L(a)-\int_D\kappa_ta|<\varepsilon/2$.

If $\|\kappa_t\|_{L^\infty(D)}=0$, choose $\kappa=0$. Otherwise use step 1.2 with $\theta=\varepsilon/(2\|\kappa_t\|_\infty)$ and set $\kappa=\zeta\kappa_t\in C_c^\infty(D)$. The cutoff error satisfies $\sup_K|\int_D(\kappa_t-\kappa)a|\le\|\kappa_t\|_\infty\sup_K\int_D(1-\zeta)|a|<\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 2.1 proves the claim.

**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

Their product cells lie in side-$\ell$ cubes centered at their midpoints, which belong to the cells. Each has volume $N^{-D}\ge2^{-D}\ell^D$. On each of the $2D$ boundary faces perform the same $(D-1)$-dimensional partition. Every residual ball intersection has volume at most $\omega_D\rho^D$. On each face its surface intersection is contained in a $(D-1)$-dimensional ball of radius $\rho$, of measure at most $\omega_{D-1}\rho^{D-1}$. Summing over $2D$ faces and dividing by total surface area $2D$ gives boundary probability at most $\omega_{D-1}\rho^{D-1}$. The probability densities are the positive constants $1$ and $1/(2D)$ on their respective supports. These are the required upper and lower bounds with the stated small-scale range.

citations.quote: The following assertion is false under the library's bounded global Hölder norm: every bounded Lipschitz domain satisfying an exterior sphere condition at each boundary point, with a strictly elliptic operator having Hölder coefficients and nonpositive expanded zero-order coefficient, has for every Hölder forcing and continuous Dirichlet data a unique solution in $C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u$$
on $U$, where $a(x)$ is symmetric, $\xi^Ta(x)\xi\ge\lambda_0|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\lambda_0>0$, the coefficients are continuous and bounded, and $\widetilde c\le0$. There is a constant $C_L<\infty$, depending only on $U$, $\lambda_0$, and the coefficient bounds, such that every $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $L[w]\in C^0(U)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$
In particular, for any two functions $u^*,h\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$,
$$\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[u^*]-L[h]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
On every ball, $C^{2,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ therefore agrees with the finite-scaled-norm class of that dependency. This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. For finite real coefficient functions $a_{ij},b_i,c_i,d$ on $U$, the positive divergence-form expression is
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_iD_i u+du.$$
Its classical domain consists of those $u\in C^2(U)$ for which every displayed flux derivative $D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$ and $D_i(b_i u)$ exists pointwise and is finite on $U$. The classical formula assigns no value outside this domain. In particular, if each $D_i a_{ij}$ and $D_i b_i$ exists pointwise and is finite, the product rule makes every $u\in C^2(U)$ admissible and gives the nondivergence expansion

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

derivations.claim: Write $p_j=\mu(X_j)$ and $N_j=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{\{Y_i\in X_j\}}$. Since $p_j\ge c\ell^s=m^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$, we have $K\le\sqrt m$. Independence gives $\mathbb E e^{-N_j/2}=(1-p_j+p_je^{-1/2})^m\le\exp(-mp_j(1-e^{-1/2}))$. For a nonnegative random variable $Z$, $a\mathbb P(Z>a)\le\mathbb E Z$, by integrating $Z\ge a\mathbf1_{Z>a}$. Apply this with $Z=e^{-N_j/2}$ and $a=e^{-mp_j/4}$ to get $\mathbb P(N_j<mp_j/2)\le\exp(mp_j/4-mp_j(1-e^{-1/2}))\le e^{-mp_j/8}$. Here $e^{1/2}\ge1+1/2+1/8=13/8>8/5$ implies $e^{-1/2}<5/8$, and $1-x\le e^{-x}$ follows by differentiating $e^{-x}-1+x$.

The event $N_j<\sqrt m/2$ is contained in $N_j<mp_j/2$. By step 1.1 and [F2], its union over cells has probability at most $K e^{-\sqrt m/8}\le\sqrt m e^{-\sqrt m/8}$. This proves the probability assertion, with the trivial lower bound zero when necessary.

On the complementary event fix $x\in X_j$. Every sample $Y_i\in X_j$ is within $\delta$ of $x$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

derivations.claim: If $U=\varnothing$, both spaces are zero and the conclusions hold. Otherwise choose finite $a<b$ with $U\subset\{a<x_1<b\}$. The zero extension of any $h\in H$ belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ with the same norm. Restricting the countable dense box-step family in [F1] to $U$ therefore gives a countable dense subset of $H$. The product $Z=H^{d+1}$ is a separable Hilbert space.

The map $J:H^1(U)\to Z$, $J(v)=(v,D_1v,\ldots,D_dv)$, is an isometry for the full Sobolev norm. Its range is closed: if $J(v_n)\to(v,g_1,\ldots,g_d)$ in $Z$, then for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\int vD_i\phi=\lim_n\int v_nD_i\phi=-\lim_n\int D_iv_n\phi=-\int g_i\phi$. Thus $g_i=D_iv$ weakly, so the limit is $J(v)$. A closed subspace of a Hilbert space is complete, hence $H^1(U)$ is Hilbert.

By the closure definition, $V$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(U)$ and is Hilbert. The Poincare inequality applies because $U$ is bounded in the first direction, and yields $\|Dv\|_2^2\le\|v\|_{H^1}^2\le(1+C^2)\|Dv\|_2^2$ on $V$. This proves norm equivalence and continuity of the inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$. Injectivity holds because these spaces use the same almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

A subspace $Y$ of a separable metric space $Z$ is separable under [A1]: if $(z_j)$ is dense in $Z$, the sets $Y\cap B(z_j,r)$ for positive rational $r$ form a countable base of $Y$; choose one point from every nonempty such set. Any relatively open neighborhood contains one of these sets, so the chosen points are dense. Apply this first to $J(H^1(U))\subset Z$ and then to $J(V)$; transport the dense subsets through the isometry $J$. Thus $V$ is separable.

By [F4], $C_c^\infty(U)$ is dense in $H$, and it is contained in $V$ by [F2]. Thus $V\hookrightarrow H$ is dense. The Hilbert, separability, continuity and injectivity conclusions already proved give the canonical evolution triple by [F5]. Every argument used an arbitrary bounded open $U$, so none requires a boundary chart or a polyhedral boundary.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$
and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling:
$\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there,
$\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$
there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with
$|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for
all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and
$(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let $\Gamma$ be the causal
extension of the heat kernel. Then
$\Gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^{n+1})$, and its regular distribution
$u_\Gamma\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^{n+1})$ satisfies
$(\partial_t-\Delta)u_\Gamma=\delta_{(0,0)}$, that is,
$$\langle(\partial_t-\Delta)u_\Gamma,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(0,0)\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{n+1}),$$
so the causal extension is a fundamental solution of $\partial_t-\Delta$.
Moreover $\Gamma(\cdot,t)\to\delta_0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ as
$t\downarrow0^+$, that is, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\varphi(x)\,dx\to\varphi(0)$
for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$. The derivative $\partial_t$ is
the distributional derivative in the last space-time coordinate.

If $K\subseteq U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq U$.

derivations.claim: Fix a constant symmetric matrix $A_0$ with eigenvalues in $[\lambda,\Lambda]$. The linear substitution $x=A_0^{1/2}y$ in [F1] gives $$G(x,t)=\mathbf1_{t>0}(4\pi t)^{-d/2}(\det A_0)^{-1/2}\exp\bigl(-x^TA_0^{-1}x/(4t)\bigr),\qquad (\partial_t-A_0:D^2)G=\delta.$$ Put $N=d+2$ and $K_{ij}=D_{ij}G$. Direct differentiation gives $|K_{ij}(z)|\le C\rho(z,0)^{-N}$, $|D_xK_{ij}(z)|\le C\rho(z,0)^{-N-1}$ and $|\partial_tK_{ij}(z)|\le C\rho(z,0)^{-N-2}$ away from zero, with Gaussian decay as $|x|/\sqrt t$ increases. The extension across $t=0$ is smooth away from $x=0$, since that decay dominates every power. The constants are uniform over $A_0$ in the given ellipticity interval.

For use with cutoffs, the following interpolation estimate holds on nested cylinders, with norms scaled to their outer radius $r$: for each $\varepsilon>0$, the scaled lower-order $\alpha$ norms of $u$ and $rDu$ are at most $\varepsilon r^2(\|D^2u\|_{\alpha;r}+\|u_t\|_{\alpha;r})+C_\varepsilon\|u\|_\infty$, provided the finite difference segments lie in the larger cylinder. To verify it, write $D_iu(x,t)$ as a centered first difference of step $\theta r$ plus its Taylor integral remainder, bounded by $C\theta r\|D^2u\|_\infty$. Apply the same identity to differences between two points. For separations smaller than $\theta r$ use the top Hölder norms, and for larger separations use the supremum estimate and divide by the separation to the power $\alpha$. For time differences of $u$ use $|t-s|\|u_t\|_\infty$. For time differences of $Du$ use spatial first differences of step $\sqrt{|t-s|}$, bounding their time difference by $C\sqrt{|t-s|}\|u_t\|_\infty$ and the two remainders by $C\sqrt{|t-s|}\|D^2u\|_\infty$; then split at $|t-s|=\theta^2r^2$. The coefficients of the top norms are positive powers of $\theta$ because $\alpha<1$. Choosing $\theta$ small makes them at most $\varepsilon$; the larger-separation terms have finite constants depending on that $\theta$ and the cylinder separation.

Each positive-time spatial integral of $K_{ij}$ is zero. Its improper integrals on parabolic balls have a bound independent of the radius. Indeed integration of $D_{ij}G$ over $|x|<R$ gives a boundary integral of $D_jG$; its absolute value is at most $CR^dt^{-d/2-1}\exp(-cR^2/t)$. Integration for $0<t<R^2$, followed by $t=R^2s$, is bounded by $C\int_0^1s^{-d/2-1}e^{-c/s}ds<\infty$. The integral is independent of $R$ by scaling. Differences of two such truncations, hence the integrals on centered parabolic annuli, are bounded uniformly as well. This is the cancellation needed at the singularity; an absolute integral of $|K_{ij}|$ there is not asserted.

Let $v\in C_c^\infty$ have support in a parabolic cylinder of radius at most $r$ and put $F_0=v_t-A_0:D^2v$. Integrating the derivative of the Gaussian convolution from a time before the support gives $v=G*F_0$: the initial convolution is zero, its derivative is convolution with $F_0$, and the positive-time approximate identity gives the upper endpoint. This uses only [F1] and differentiation of smooth compactly supported functions. Differentiation of this identity expresses $D_{ij}v$ as the principal-value convolution with $K_{ij}$, with a fixed bounded constant multiple of $F_0$ if the truncation is by parabolic balls rather than positive time strips. That constant is the radius-independent truncation integral in step 2.1.

The singular-integral estimates follow directly as follows. At a pole subtract $F_0$ evaluated at that pole. On an annulus of radius $s$, the difference is bounded by $[F_0]_\alpha s^\alpha$, and its absolute integral against $K_{ij}$ is at most $C[F_0]_\alpha s^\alpha$. For two poles at parabolic distance $h$, the parts within distance $4h$ of either pole are therefore bounded by $C[F_0]_\alpha\int_0^{4h}s^{\alpha-1}ds\le C[F_0]_\alpha h^\alpha$. On the complement use the same subtracted constant at both poles. The kernel difference is at most $Chs^{-N-1}$: spatial displacement follows from $D_xK_{ij}$, and time displacement, of size at most $h^2$, from $\partial_tK_{ij}$ and $h^2s^{-N-2}\le hs^{-N-1}$. Its integral is bounded by $C[F_0]_\alpha h\int_{4h}^\infty s^{\alpha-2}ds\le C[F_0]_\alpha h^\alpha$. Changing the near-region truncation produces annular pieces controlled by these same estimates; changing the subtracted constant produces at most $C|F_0(z)-F_0(z')|$ by step 2.1. Thus $[D^2v]_\alpha\le C[F_0]_\alpha$. On the support neighborhood, integrating only up to radius comparable with $r$ and using the bounded truncation term gives $\|D^2v\|_\infty\le C(\|F_0\|_\infty+r^\alpha[F_0]_\alpha)$; outside that neighborhood the kernel is nonsingular and its Gaussian bound gives the same estimate. The compact time support may be used to truncate all time integrals before subtraction, so no absolutely divergent integral at infinite time is introduced.

Since $v_t=F_0+A_0:D^2v$, the same bounds hold for $v_t$. In the scaled notation $\|g\|_{\alpha;r}=\|g\|_\infty+r^\alpha[g]_\alpha$, the result is $$r^2\bigl(\|D^2v\|_{\alpha;r}+\|v_t\|_{\alpha;r}\bigr)\le Cr^2\|v_t-A_0:D^2v\|_{\alpha;r}.$$ All constants depend only on $d,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the fixed support-radius multiple. The strict inequality $\alpha<1$ is used in the convergent far integral of step 4.1.

Choose a cutoff $\eta$ supported in a cylinder of radius $r$ near $z_0$, and put $v=\eta u$, extended by zero. Freeze $A_0=A(z_0)$. Leibniz's formula gives $$v_t-A_0:D^2v=\eta F+(A-A_0):D^2v+\beta\cdot Dv+qv+u(\eta_t-A:D^2\eta-\beta\cdot D\eta)-2(A D\eta)\cdot Du.$$ The scaled product norm of $(A-A_0):D^2v$ is bounded by $Cr^\alpha[A]_\alpha\|D^2v\|_{\alpha;r}$. Choose $r$ so that this coefficient, multiplied by the constant in step 5.1, is at most $1/4$, and absorb it there. The remaining drift, zero-order and cutoff terms involve only $u,Du$ and $F$; step 1.2 absorbs their top-norm contributions after choosing its $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small. Cutoffs with derivatives bounded by powers of the inverse gap between inner and outer cylinders are supplied by [F2] after rescaling.

The resulting nested-cylinder inequality has the form $M(s)\le\varepsilon M(S)+C_\varepsilon(S-s)^{-m}B$, where $M$ is the full scaled top norm, $m<\infty$ is fixed and $B=\|u\|_\infty+\|F\|_\alpha$. To remove the outer top norm, choose radii $s_j=s_0+a(1-2^{-j})$ whose limiting cylinder is strictly inside the domain, and take $\varepsilon<2^{-m-1}$. Iteration gives a convergent geometric sum of the $B$ terms. The remainder $\varepsilon^jM(s_j)$ tends to zero because $u$ is smooth on the fixed larger compact cylinder. Thus $M(s_0)\le CB$. A finite cover of $K$ by the small cylinders in step 6.1, and step 1.2 for the lower derivatives, gives the stated estimate. The choices used coefficient Hölder bounds and ellipticity only, proving the asserted independence from higher coefficient derivatives.
