citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge2$, and let $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ satisfy
$0<\alpha<1$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and compactly
supported, with finite global Hölder seminorm
$$[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}:=\sup_{x\ne y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}<\infty.$$
This is the convention for $f\in C_c^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^n)$ here; the
positive-base real power is as in [[def-real-power]]. Put
$\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{\mathbb R^n}|f|+[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}$.
Then the Newtonian integral from [[def-newtonian-potential]] is absolutely
finite for every $x$, belongs to $C^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and its second derivatives
are locally $\alpha$-Hölder continuous. In particular
$Nf\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^n)$, where this notation means that
$Nf$ is $C^2$ and each second partial derivative has finite $\alpha$-Hölder
seminorm on every compact set. Moreover,
$$-\Delta Nf(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).$$
For every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and every $r>0$ with
$\operatorname{supp}f\subset B_r(x)$, the absolutely convergent cancellation
formula is
$$\partial_i\partial_jNf(x)=\int_{B_r(x)}\partial_i\partial_j\Phi(x-y)\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)\,dy-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{n}f(x),\qquad 0\le i,j<n.$$
For each compact $K\subset\mathbb R^n$, a constant depending only on $n$, $\alpha$
and bounds for $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}f$ satisfies
$$\max_{|\beta|\le2}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\beta Nf(x)|+\max_{|\beta|=2}[\partial^\beta Nf]_{\alpha;K}\le C\,\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}.$$

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge3$. For every real or complex $g\in C(\partial B_R(a))$ the integral
$$U_g(x)=\int_{\partial B_R(a)}P_{R,a}(x,y)g(y)\,dS_y$$
is absolutely convergent, smooth and harmonic on $B_R(a)$, and $U_g$ extends continuously to $\overline{B_R(a)}$ with boundary trace $g$. It is the unique function in $C^2(B_R(a))\cap C(\overline{B_R(a)})$ that is harmonic on $B_R(a)$ and equals $g$ on $\partial B_R(a)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, $R>0$, and $g\in C^\infty(\partial B_R(a))$ be real. Write $\omega_{n-1}=|S^{n-1}|$. There is a unique $h\in C^\infty(B_R(a))\cap C(\overline B_R(a))$ harmonic inside and equal to $g$ on the sphere. It is
$$h(x)=\int_{\partial B_R(a)}\frac{R^2-|x-a|^2}{R\omega_{n-1}|x-y|^n}\,g(y)\,dS(y),\qquad |x-a|<R.$$
The kernel is positive and has integral one at each interior point.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $u$ be real or complex harmonic on $\Omega$, let $B_r(x)\Subset\Omega$ with $r>0$, and let $\alpha$ be a multi-index. Then
$$\bigl|D^\alpha u(x)\bigr|\le C_{n,\alpha}\,r^{-n-|\alpha|}\int_{B_r(x)}|u(y)|\,dy,$$
where the constant $C_{n,\alpha}$ depends only on $n$ and $\alpha$, not on $u$, $x$, $r$ or $\Omega$.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, nonempty and open. If $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and $\Delta u\ge0$, then
$$\max_{\overline\Omega}u=\max_{\partial\Omega}u.$$
No connectedness or boundary smoothness is required.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.

Let $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^k$, $k\ge1$, and let $c$ be a regular value. Near each point, a regular level set is a $C^k$ graph over $\ker Df(a)$ of dimension $m-n$.

More precisely, for $a\in f^{-1}(c)$ put $K=\ker Df(a)$ and $E=K^\perp$, so $\mathbb R^m=K\oplus E$. There are neighbourhoods $P\subseteq K$ of $0$ and $Q\subseteq E$ of $0$ and a $C^k$ map $g:P\to Q$ with $g(0)=0$ and $Dg(0)=0$ such that, near $a$,
$$f^{-1}(c)=\{a+u+g(u):u\in P\}.$$
The empty fibre satisfies the regular-value convention vacuously, and when $m=n$ the local graph has zero-dimensional domain and is the isolated point $a$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
On every ball, $C^{2,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ therefore agrees with the finite-scaled-norm class of that dependency. This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $k=n-1\ge1$, $0<\alpha<1$, and $$P_t(z)=c_k\frac{t}{(|z|^2+t^2)^{(k+1)/2}},\qquad Q_{j,t}(z)=c_k\frac{z_j}{(|z|^2+t^2)^{(k+1)/2}},$$ where $c_k$ is the reciprocal of $\int_{\mathbb R^k}(1+|z|^2)^{-(k+1)/2}dz$. This integral is finite by polar integration: its radial behavior is $r^{k-1}$ at zero and $r^{-2}$ at infinity. Thus $P_t$ is nonnegative, has mass one by scaling, and its usual differentiation verifies harmonicity in $(z,t)$. The formulas apply also when $n=2$, $k=1$; no $n\ge3$ half-space theorem is assumed.

We first prove the elementary singular-kernel estimate required below. If $a\in C_c^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^k)$ has support in a fixed ball, then on every fixed bounded cylinder $|x|\le R$, $0\le t\le R$ the functions $$T_{j,t}a(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^k}Q_{j,t}(z)a(x-z)dz\quad(t>0)$$ extend continuously to $t=0$ and satisfy $$\|T_ja\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{\mathcal C_R})}\le C\|a\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^k)}.$$ Here the boundary integral is the absolutely convergent cancellation expression $$T_{j,0}a(x)=\int_{|z|<1}Q_{j,0}(z)(a(x-z)-a(x))dz+\int_{|z|\ge1}Q_{j,0}(z)a(x-z)dz.$$ Indeed the kernels are odd in $z$, their integrals over every centered annulus vanish, and uniformly in $t\ge0$, $$|Q_{j,t}(z)|\le C|z|^{-k},\qquad |D_zQ_{j,t}(z)|+|\partial_tQ_{j,t}(z)|\le C|z|^{-k-1}\quad(z\ne0).$$ The near part of the displayed cancellation integral is bounded by $C[a]_\alpha\int_0^1r^{\alpha-1}dr$. For bounded $x$, the far integral lies in a fixed annulus and is bounded by $C_R\|a\|_\infty$; this proves the supremum bound uniformly in $t$.

Here are the complete difference estimates. For a vertical change $|t-s|=\delta<1/8$, subtract $a(x)$ under the integral on $|z|<1$ using oddness. The part $|z|<2\delta$ is bounded by $C[a]_\alpha\delta^\alpha$. On $2\delta<|z|<1$, the mean value estimate for $\partial_tQ$ bounds the difference by $$C[a]_\alpha\delta\int_{2\delta}^1r^{\alpha-2}dr\le C_\alpha[a]_\alpha\delta^\alpha.$$ The far part costs $C_R\|a\|_\infty\delta$, hence also $C_R\|a\|_\infty\delta^\alpha$. The same argument with $s=0$ proves convergence to the boundary expression.

For a horizontal change $|x-y|=\delta<1/8$ at fixed height, write both operators in the physical integration variable $\zeta$, subtract respectively $a(x)$ and $a(y)$ in unit balls centered at their poles, and split at the union of the two radius-$2\delta$ balls. The near pieces cost $C[a]_\alpha\delta^\alpha$, since each pole is at most $3\delta$ from the other near ball. On the common far region inside the unit balls, use $$|Q_t(x-\zeta)-Q_t(y-\zeta)|\le C\delta|x-\zeta|^{-k-1}$$ and $|a(\zeta)-a(x)|\le[a]_\alpha|x-\zeta|^\alpha$. Its integral is the same $C[a]_\alpha\delta\int_{2\delta}^{2}r^{\alpha-2}dr$ as above. The remaining constant-difference term is $a(x)-a(y)$ times an integral of $Q_t$ over the far integration region. That integral is uniformly bounded: compare its domain to a centered annulus, whose integral is zero. At the inner boundary the symmetric difference is contained in a shell of radius at most $4\delta$ and outside radius $\delta$, of volume $C\delta^k$ and kernel bound $C\delta^{-k}$; its integral is $O(1)$. At the outer boundary the symmetric difference has volume $C\delta$ and bounded kernel, also $O(1)$. These bounds use only the stated kernel estimates, uniformly in $t$. Multiplying by $|a(x)-a(y)|\le[a]_\alpha\delta^\alpha$ gives the required bound. Outside the unit neighborhoods the kernels and their first derivatives are bounded on the fixed support region, so that part is Lipschitz with constant $C_R\|a\|_\infty$; the moving unit-boundary shells have the same bound after the cancellation constants are included. This proves horizontal $\alpha$-Hölder control. Larger increments are covered by the supremum bound. Combining a horizontal and a vertical change proves the asserted joint Hölder estimate.

The Poisson operator itself maps bounded $C^\alpha$ data to $C^\alpha$ on the closed half-space, locally with controlled norm. Horizontal differences follow by translation and its mass one. For vertical differences, differentiating the explicit kernel and scaling gives $$\int|\partial_tP_t(z)|\,|z|^\alpha dz\le C_\alpha t^{\alpha-1},\qquad\int\partial_tP_t=0.$$ The moment is finite since $\alpha<1$. Thus $|\partial_t(P_t*a)|\le C[a]_\alpha t^{\alpha-1}$; integration from $s$ to $t$ gives $C[a]_\alpha|t-s|^\alpha$. The same moment estimate for $P_t$ proves its convergence to $a$ at $t=0$ with error $C[a]_\alpha t^\alpha$.

Now let $\phi\in C_c^{2,\alpha}(\mathbb R^k)$. Set $H(x,t)=P_t*\phi(x)$. Differentiation under the integral for $t>0$, followed by tangential integration by parts, gives $D_aH=P_t*D_a\phi$ and $D_{ab}H=P_t*D_{ab}\phi$. The explicit identities $$\partial_tP_t=-\sum_{j=1}^k\partial_jQ_{j,t},\qquad\Delta_{x,t}P_t=0$$ give $$D_tD_aH=-\sum_jQ_{j,t}*D_{ja}\phi,\qquad D_{tt}H=-\sum_aP_t*D_{aa}\phi.$$ The same identity without $D_a$ bounds $D_tH$ by the $T_j$ estimates applied to $D_j\phi$. Each datum on the right is compactly supported $C^\alpha$. The just-proved $P$ and $T$ bounds show that $H$, its gradient and Hessian extend to the boundary, with Hessian $\alpha$-Hölder there and $$\|H\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{\mathcal C_R})}\le C\|\phi\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\mathbb R^k)}.$$ Classical derivatives up to the boundary mean the continuous interior derivative extensions; their compatibility follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus along interior coordinate segments and then passage to the boundary. No Riesz-transform boundedness theorem or unproved mixed-derivative claim has been cited.

Write $B_r^+=B_r\cap\{x_n>0\}$ and its flat face $B_r'=B_r\cap\{x_n=0\}$. If $u\in C^2(B_1^+)\cap C(\overline{B_1^+})$, $\Delta u=f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_1^+})$, and $u=0$ on $B_1'$, then $$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\overline{B_{1/4}^+})}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_1^+}+\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_1^+})}\bigr).$$ To prove this, extend $f$ evenly across the flat face on $B_1$, and multiply by a smooth cutoff supported in $B_1$ and equal to one on $B_{3/4}$. The even extension is Hölder: if the two points are on opposite sides, the distance between their reflected upper-half-space points is no greater than their original distance. Thus the resulting $F\in C_c^\alpha(\mathbb R^n)$ has controlled norm. The actual local theorem `thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical` gives $v=-NF$, with $\Delta v=f$ on $B_{3/4}^+$ and $\|v\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar B_{3/4})}\le C\|f\|_{C^\alpha}$. This theorem covers $n=2$ with its logarithmic kernel, and no boundedness of $v$ at infinity is required.

The continuous ball-Dirichlet supplier currently has dimension restriction $n\ge3$. For $n=2$ the needed continuous-data disk solution follows from the actual $n\ge2$ supplier `lem-smooth-sphere-data-have-a-harmonic-replacement` as follows. Parametrize the boundary circle by angle and extend its continuous datum to a continuous $2\pi$-periodic function $a(\theta)$. Convolve in the angle with a nonnegative smooth periodic unit-mass kernel supported, modulo $2\pi$, in $|\theta|<\epsilon$. The result $a_\epsilon$ is smooth and periodic, and $\|a_\epsilon-a\|_\infty\le\sup_{|h|\le\epsilon,\theta}|a(\theta-h)-a(\theta)|\to0$ by uniform continuity on the circle. The smooth-sphere supplier gives harmonic $H_\epsilon$ continuous on the closed disk with these data. The weak maximum principle gives $\|H_\epsilon-H_\eta\|_{\infty;\bar B}\le\|a_\epsilon-a_\eta\|_\infty$, so $H_\epsilon$ converges uniformly on the closed disk to a continuous function with the prescribed boundary datum. Interior derivative estimates applied to the differences show that all derivatives converge uniformly on smaller disks; the fundamental theorem of calculus identifies them as the derivatives of the uniform limit, which is therefore harmonic. Uniqueness follows from the weak maximum principle. This supplies continuous ball data in dimension two without extending a dimension-restricted theorem silently.

Choose a tangential cutoff equal to one on $B_{2/3}'$ and supported in $B_{3/4}'$, and put $\phi$ equal to that cutoff times $v|_{x_n=0}$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^{n-1}$. the Poisson-extension calculation above gives a harmonic $H=P\phi$ with controlled $C^{2,\alpha}$ norm on $\overline{B_{2/3}^+}$. The remainder $w=u-v+H$ is harmonic in $B_{2/3}^+$, continuous on its closure and zero on its flat face. Its odd extension is harmonic in $B_{1/2}$. Here is a proof requiring no boundary derivatives of $u$: on each ball centered on the flat face and compactly contained in $B_{2/3}$, solve the ordinary ball Dirichlet problem for the continuous odd boundary data obtained from $w$; uniqueness on the ball makes its solution odd, and uniqueness by the weak maximum principle on the upper half-ball identifies it with $w$. Thus the odd extension is harmonic near every plane point, as well as off the plane.

The actual harmonic interior derivative estimates on $B_{1/2}$ bound its derivatives through order three on $B_{1/4}$ by $C\|w\|_{\infty;B_{1/2}^+}$. A third derivative bound gives the required second derivative $\alpha$-Hölder bound on that ball, since $\alpha<1$. Combining this with the $v,H$ bounds proves the half-ball estimate, and at the same time proves its boundary regularity upgrade noncircularly for the Laplacian.

Rescaling gives the corresponding estimate between $B_r^+$ and $B_{r/4}^+$ in scaled norms. It holds for every constant symmetric positive definite principal matrix $A_0$ with $\lambda I\le A_0\le\Lambda I$, with constants depending only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and a fixed target-radius fraction. To see that the linear normalization preserves the boundary plane, take $S=A_0^{1/2}$, choose an orthogonal matrix $O$ whose last column is $Se_n/|Se_n|$, and set $T=SO$. Then $TT^T=A_0$ and $(Ty)_n=|Se_n|y_n$. Therefore $A_0:D_x^2$ becomes $\Delta_y$ under $x=Ty$, and upper half-spaces map onto upper half-spaces. The singular values of $T$ lie in $[\sqrt\lambda,\sqrt\Lambda]$, so contained/containing half-balls have fixed comparable radii. Restricting the estimate to the contained smaller half-ball gives the assertion.

This section is intentionally an **a priori** statement: let $V$ have smooth boundary but a uniformly controlled finite $C^{2,\alpha}$ graph atlas, let $A,\beta,c$ be smooth near $\bar V$ with uniform $C^\alpha$ bounds and ellipticity, and let $u$ be smooth to the boundary, zero on the boundary, with $Lu=F$. Then $$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar V)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_\infty+\|F\|_{C^\alpha(\bar V)}\bigr),$$ where $C$ depends on the uniform atlas, the coefficient Hölder bounds, ellipticity, dimension and exponent, but not on higher smoothness norms.

A smooth graph flattening $x=\Psi(y)$ transforms the equation to $\widetilde A:D_y^2w+\widetilde\beta\cdot D_yw+\widetilde c w=\widetilde F$ with $w=u\circ\Psi$ and zero flat trace. The chain rule expresses $\widetilde A=D\Psi^{-1}A(D\Psi^{-1})^T$ and the drift as the transformed original drift plus $A:D_x^2\Psi^{-1}$. The uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ chart bounds give uniform ellipticity and $C^\alpha$ bounds for every transformed coefficient. Thus no derivative of the original coefficients beyond the stated Hölder bound enters this estimate.

Fix a small common chart radius $r$. On each boundary patch freeze $\widetilde A$ at its flat-face center and apply the constant-coefficient half-ball estimate on an ambient half-ball of radius comparable to $r$; on interior balls use the corresponding constant-coefficient full-ball estimate, which follows directly from the local Newtonian potential and harmonic remainder argument. For the frozen forcing use $$\widetilde A_0:D^2w=\widetilde F+(\widetilde A_0-\widetilde A):D^2w-\widetilde\beta\cdot Dw-\widetilde c w.$$ There is no regularity issue in this application, since $w$ is already smooth on the closed half-patch.

Use the common scaled global norm $$N_r(u)=\|u\|_\infty+r\|Du\|_\infty+r^2\|D^2u\|_\infty+r^{2+\alpha}[D^2u]_\alpha.$$ The product inequality $[pq]_\alpha\le\|p\|_\infty[q]_\alpha+[p]_\alpha\|q\|_\infty$, the freezing bounds $\|\widetilde A-\widetilde A_0\|_\infty\le Kr^\alpha$, $[\widetilde A]_\alpha\le K$, and the convex-half-ball estimate $[Dw]_\alpha\le C r^{1-\alpha}\|D^2w\|_\infty$ show that the scaled frozen error is at most $$C\bigl(Kr^\alpha+r\|\widetilde\beta\|_\infty+r^{1+\alpha}[\widetilde\beta]_\alpha+r^2\|\widetilde c\|_\infty+r^{2+\alpha}[\widetilde c]_\alpha\bigr)\,N_r(u)=:\eta(r)N_r(u).$$ Chart norm comparison changes $C$ only by uniform atlas constants; the terms from second chart derivatives times $Du$ carry a factor $r$ and are controlled in the same way. In particular $\eta(r)\to0$ uniformly over the stated family.

For precision, gluing the patch estimates costs a fixed constant independent of the number of patches. Take a finite cover by their smaller inner patches and interior balls, with a Lebesgue number at least $c_0r$, using the common graph radii and a lattice of balls of radius a fixed multiple of $r$; the constant $c_0>0$ depends only on the uniform atlas distortion. Supremum derivative norms are bounded by the maximum of the corresponding local norms, with the uniform chart comparisons. If $|x-y|<c_0r$, the pair lies in one inner patch and its Hessian quotient is controlled there. If $|x-y|\ge c_0r$, its contribution to $r^{2+\alpha}[D^2u]_\alpha$ is at most $2c_0^{-\alpha}r^2\|D^2u\|_\infty$. Thus $$N_r(u)\le C_0\bigl(\|u\|_\infty+r^2\|F\|_\infty+r^{2+\alpha}[F]_\alpha\bigr)+C_1\eta(r)N_r(u).$$ The constants $C_0,C_1$ are uniform; no sum over all covering balls occurs. Choose the common radius so $C_1\eta(r)\le1/2$ and absorb the final term. Since $r$ is now fixed in terms of the permitted data, the unscaled asserted global estimate follows. This argument proves the estimate only for the smooth functions to which it was applied; a consuming existence proof obtains the original solution's regularity by passing this estimate to a limit.

A bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain $U$ has a global $C^{2,\alpha}$ defining function $\rho$ on $\mathbb R^n$, equal to $1$ outside a large ball and to $-1$ away from a collar inside $U$, with $U=\{\rho<0\}$ and $|D\rho|\ge c>0$ near $\partial U$. Here is a construction. On a finite boundary atlas use the signed graph functions $\rho_\ell=x_n-h_\ell(x')$, after rigid motions, each negative inside. Choose a smooth partition of unity on a collar subordinate to those chart neighborhoods and put $\rho_0=\sum\chi_\ell\rho_\ell$. On the boundary, the gradients of the signed graph functions are positive scalar multiples of the same outward unit normal; the terms $D\chi_\ell\rho_\ell$ vanish there. Therefore $D\rho_0\ne0$ on the boundary, with a uniform lower bound by compactness. Every active signed graph function has the same sign on each side, so $\rho_0$ has exactly the correct sign in a sufficiently small collar. Multiply by a smooth collar cutoff equal to one in a smaller collar, and outside use the sign function $-1$ on $U$, $+1$ outside. The latter is multiplied by a function identically zero near the boundary, so this gluing is $C^{2,\alpha}$ globally and introduces no new zeros. Shrinking the collar preserves the gradient lower bound. All derivatives and their Hölder bounds are finite because only finitely many compactly supported chart pieces occur.

Let $\rho_j=\rho*\rho_{s_j}$ for $s_j\downarrow0$, and put $a_j=\max\{j^{-1},\|\rho_j-\rho\|_{C^1}\}$. Mollification gives $a_j\to0$, uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bounds on $\rho_j$ and $C^2$ convergence to $\rho$; the latter follows from uniform continuity of $D^2\rho$. Define $$V_j=\{\rho_j<-2a_j\}.$$ For large $j$, its boundary lies in the fixed collar, where $|D\rho_j|\ge c/2$. Hence $V_j$ has smooth boundary, $\bar V_j\subset U$, and every compact subset of $U$ eventually lies inside $V_j$. It is bounded since $\rho_j=1$ outside a fixed large ball. No regular-value selection is needed for this particular smooth-boundary approximation.

These domains have a common finite atlas with uniformly bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ graph norms. Indeed, after shrinking the original charts, choose in each a coordinate with $|\partial_n\rho|\ge c_1>0$. Uniform $C^1$ convergence gives $|\partial_n\rho_j|\ge c_1/2$, so the level equations $\rho_j(x',h_j(x'))=-2a_j$ have graphs on fixed smaller chart cylinders, by monotonicity in the normal coordinate and the intermediate value theorem. Their derivative formulas are $$D_ah_j=-\frac{\rho_{j,a}}{\rho_{j,n}},$$ $$D_{ab}h_j=-\frac{\rho_{j,ab}+\rho_{j,an}D_bh_j+\rho_{j,bn}D_ah_j+\rho_{j,nn}D_ah_jD_bh_j}{\rho_{j,n}}.$$ The denominator stays bounded away from zero, the second derivatives of $\rho_j$ have uniform Hölder bounds, and the first derivative formulas give uniform Lipschitz bounds for the graphs and their first derivatives. Product, quotient and composition Hölder estimates then give the uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bounds. Compactness and convergence place all of $\partial V_j$ in these fixed smaller cylinders. This proves every geometric property needed by the freezing and gluing argument, rather than invoking an unproved smooth-domain-approximation theorem.

The freezing and gluing argument proves the uniform a priori estimate for precisely the smooth solutions specified in the Statement, and the defining-function construction supplies the required smooth interior approximating domains with the uniform atlas controls needed by that estimate. The half-ball estimate and the Poisson mixed derivative bounds were derived by the kernel calculation and reflection above; they were not assumed as external analytic results. Both conclusions follow.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $d\ge1$, and put $H=L^2(U;\mathbb R)$ and $V=H^1_0(U;\mathbb R)$, where the latter is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(U)$. Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, its inclusion into $H$ is continuous, injective and dense, and $(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple. The gradient norm and the full $H^1$ norm are equivalent on $V$. No regularity of $\partial U$ is required.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded and open, $T>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. At every $x_0\in\partial U$ assume there is an exterior tangent closed ball, disjoint from $U$ and containing $x_0$ on its sphere. Let $A=A^T$, $\beta,q,f$ be bounded on $U\times(0,T]$, locally parabolic $\alpha$-Hölder up to its final face, with $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$, $\lambda>0$, and $q\le0$. Let the combined initial and lateral datum $\psi$ be continuous on $\Gamma_T=(\bar U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T])$, including compatibility at their intersection. Then there is a unique
$$u\in C^{2+\alpha,1+\alpha/2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U\times(0,T])\cap C(\bar U\times[0,T])$$
with $-u_t+A:D^2u+\beta\cdot Du+qu=f$ and $u=\psi$ on $\Gamma_T$. It obeys $\|u\|_\infty\le\|\psi\|_\infty+T\|f\|_\infty$. Moreover it is the interior limit of smooth-coefficient weak solutions on finite polyhedral subdomains exhausting $U$, with uniform supremum bounds and the uniform compact-interior estimates just stated. If the coefficients possess a bounded divergence representation compatible in distributions, those approximants may be chosen by convolution of its original divergence coefficients.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Every bounded sequence in a separable real Hilbert
space $X$ has a weakly convergent subsequence. If $V$ is a separable real
Hilbert space, then $L^2(0,T;V)$ and $L^2(0,T;V^*)$ are separable real Hilbert
spaces, their product is a separable Hilbert space, and the graph of the weak
time-derivative operator is closed there. Consequently $W(0,T;V)$ is a closed
Hilbert subspace of that product and every bounded sequence in $W(0,T;V)$ has
a weakly convergent subsequence.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

derivations.claim: Use the domains $U_n$ and divergence-compatible smooth convolution approximants from [F2], with zero initial and lateral data and source $r_n$. Their spatial mollifier support stays inside $U$ at every point of $U_n$; their temporal mollifier is supported at positive past lags, sampling $t-s$ with $s>0$. Thus $a_n$ retains ellipticity and its bound, $b_n,c_n,d_n$ retain their separate bounds, and the expanded $\beta_n,q_n$ are the convolutions of the bounded original expanded coefficients, retaining their bounds and $q_n\le0$. No endpoint limit of the original $b,c,d$ at $T$ is used. Each fixed smooth approximant may be extended locally past $T$ for its construction; compactness is used only at times below $T$. The resulting weak solutions $e_n$ are smooth in the interior, uniformly bounded, and have a locally classical subsequential limit with zero continuous initial/lateral data at every time below $T$ by [F2]. Classical comparison on cylinders ending below $T$ identifies the limit with $e$.

Test the weak equation $e_{n,t}-L_ne_n=-r_n$ with $e_n$. The divergence terms have no boundary contribution because $e_n\in H^1_0(U_n)$ in time-integrated sense. In particular the lower-order spatial form is $$\int_{U_n}a_nDe_n\cdot De_n+\int_{U_n}(b_n-c_n)\cdot De_n\,e_n-\int_{U_n}d_ne_n^2.$$ The cross term is $b_n-c_n$, since the $b$ term is integrated by parts and the $c$ term is not. Write $B=\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty$ and $D=\|d\|_\infty$. With $y_n=\|e_n\|_2^2$, [F3], ellipticity and Young's inequality give $$\frac12y_n'+\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\|De_n\|_2^2\le\left(\frac{B^2}{2\lambda_0}+D+\frac12\right)y_n+\frac12\|r_n\|_2^2.$$ The constants are uniform in $n$; derivatives of the smoothed coefficients do not occur.

Put $C_0=B^2/\lambda_0+2D+1$. The previous inequality gives $y_n'+\lambda_0\|De_n\|_2^2\le C_0y_n+\|r_n\|_2^2$. Multiply by $e^{-C_0t}$ and integrate, using $y_n(0)=0$. Then $\sup_ty_n\le e^{C_0T}\|r_n\|_{L^2}^2$. Integrating the same differential inequality without the factor bounds $\lambda_0\int\|De_n\|_2^2$ by $C_0T\sup y_n+\|r_n\|_{L^2}^2$. The boundedness of $r$ and the finite cylinder give a uniform right side.

Extend each $e_n$ by zero from $U_n$ to $U$. For almost every time this lies in $H^1_0(U)$: extend its compactly supported smooth $H^1(U_n)$ approximants by zero, which preserves their norms, and use the closure definition in [F1]. The bounds in step 3.1 therefore give a bounded sequence in $L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$. Apply [F4] and pass to a weakly convergent subsequence. The local uniform convergence from step 1.1 identifies this weak limit with $e$ almost everywhere, by testing on compact interior cylinders. Such cylinders exhaust $U\times(0,T)$; a locally zero $L^2$ function is zero almost everywhere on their union. Hence $e\in L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$.

Fix a compact positive-time cylinder $K\Subset U\times(0,T)$ and a smooth spacetime cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near $K$. Extend each of $\chi b,\chi c,\chi d$ by zero to $\mathbb R^{d+1}$; these bounded compactly supported functions belong to $L^2$. The nonnegative product convolution kernels used in step 1.1 have mass one, $L^1$ norm one, and support shrinking to zero in both space and time (with positive past time lag). Thus they satisfy the approximate-identity conditions, although the spatial and temporal scales differ. Apply [F5] with $p=2$ to these extensions. For large $n$ their convolutions agree on $K$ with $b_n,c_n,d_n$, respectively, so $b_n\to b$, $c_n\to c$ and $d_n\to d$ strongly in $L^2(K)$, with their common uniform supremum bounds. Only $a_n,\beta_n,q_n,r_n$ are asserted to converge uniformly on such compact cylinders, by their local Hölder regularity. For a smooth test $\phi$ supported in $K$, the $a_nDe_n\cdot D\phi$ term passes by uniform coefficient convergence and weak $L^2$ gradient convergence. In the term $c_n\cdot De_n\,\phi$, the test vector $c_n\phi$ converges strongly in $L^2(K)$, so its pairing with the bounded weakly convergent gradients tends to $\int c\cdot De\,\phi$. In the $b_n e_n\cdot D\phi$ and $d_ne_n\phi$ terms, strong local coefficient convergence and local uniform convergence of $e_n$ imply strong $L^2$ convergence of the products. The source and time-test terms pass by local uniform convergence. These arguments prove the limiting weak identity on every compact positive-time cylinder without extra spatial $C^1$ assumptions on $b,c,d$.

For a smooth spacetime test with compact spatial support in $U$ but not necessarily vanishing at initial time, first perform the passage above on $[\delta,T]$, taking its support strictly below $T$ when necessary. The common bounded coefficient and source norms, supremum bounds and energy bounds control the omitted interval $(0,\delta)$ uniformly: terms linear in gradients are at most a fixed constant times $\sqrt\delta\|De_n\|_{L^2}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, and the zeroth-order, source and time-test terms are at most a constant times $\delta$. The same bounds hold for the limit by step 4.1. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ therefore gives the identity with zero initial boundary term, inherited from the approximants. Density of spatial compact-smooth functions in $H^1_0(U)$ extends the positive-time identity to all variational tests, since the divergence coefficients are bounded and the limit has the membership established in step 4.1. It follows that $e_t=L_te-r\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(U))$.

By [F3], this evolution-space function has a continuous $L^2$ trace. Its integration-by-parts identity compared with the weak identity in step 6.1, for tests $\eta(t)\phi(x)$ with $\eta(0)\ne0$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, gives $(e(0),\phi)_{L^2}=0$. Density in $L^2(U)$ gives $e(0)=0$. Thus $e$ is a zero-initial variational solution as claimed. If two such weak solutions exist, their difference has zero source and zero initial value. The same test and integrating-factor argument as steps 2.1–3.1 on $U$ gives zero $L^2$ norm at every time, proving weak uniqueness.

Apply [F3] to the now identified weak solution $e$, repeating step 2.1 on $U$ with its actual source $r$. The integrating-factor and integrated gradient arguments in step 3.1 yield the stated estimate with, for example, $C_E=e^{C_0T}+\lambda_0^{-1}(C_0Te^{C_0T}+1)$. The exact value is immaterial, but its dependence is only on the declared quantities, not on boundary derivatives of $e$.

For the final convergence assertion, $\|r_m\|_{L^2}^2\le T|U|\|r_m\|_\infty^2\to0$. The estimate in step 8.1 gives $\int\|De_m\|_2^2\to0$, and either that estimate or $\int\|e_m\|_2^2\le T|U|\|e_m\|_\infty^2$ gives the zeroth-order term. Their sum is the squared $L^2(0,T;H^1(U))$ norm. This proves strong convergence and completes the result.

citations.quote:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact, and let $f,f_n:X\to Y$ be continuous for every integer $n\ge1$. Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N\ge1$ such that $d_Y(f_n(x),f(x))<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$ and all $x\in K$.
Then
$$W=f[K]\cup\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n[K]$$
is compact in $Y$. The empty-set case is included, and the proof uses no choice principle.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]). Then $(X,d)$ is totally bounded
([[def-totally-bounded]]) and complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).

**Both implications are theorems of ZF.** Completeness is obtained here from the
finite intersection characterisation ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]])
applied to the closures of the tails of a Cauchy sequence, and not from the
extraction of a convergent subsequence, which would route the argument through
sequential compactness. What matters for the ledger is that the route taken below
selects nothing at all; the first remark below says why the other route was not
taken.

Let $A$ and $U$ be real Banach spaces of functions on bounded domains $D$ and $D'$, with the input point evaluations used below defined. For every $n\ge1$, choose finite-dimensional normed spaces $E_n,F_n$, an exactly defined sampling map $S_n:A\to E_n$ (for example, $S_n(a)=(a(\xi_{n,1}),\ldots,a(\xi_{n,N_n}))$ at specified input points), a finite-dimensional map $\widetilde G_n:E_n\to F_n$, and an output reconstruction map $R_n:F_n\to U$. The reconstruction supplies a function with a defined value at every point of $D'$. The corresponding continuum-valued discrete map is
$$G_n(a):=R_n\bigl(\widetilde G_n(S_n(a))\bigr)\in U.$$
A family $(G_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a **discretization-invariant approximation** of an operator $G:A\to U$ if its sampling maps and output reconstructions are part of the family and it approximates this single continuum operator as the input discretization is refined. In the compact-uniform version, for every compact $K\subset A$,
$$\sup_{a\in K}\|G_n(a)-G(a)\|_U\longrightarrow0.$$
For $K=\emptyset$, the supremum of this nonnegative error is defined to be $0$. When $A$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes, the sampling map must be explicitly defined on those classes or use a specified representative convention; point evaluation is not inferred from the equivalence class alone. This definition does not identify unrelated grid-specific maps as one operator family.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ and let
$(A,d_A)$ be the metric subspace ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Relative openness is a trace.** A set $V \subseteq A$ is open in $(A,d_A)$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) if and only if $V = U \cap A$ for some $U$ open in
   $(X,d)$.
2. **Compactness read in the ambient space.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$
   ([[def-metric-compactness]]), that is $(A,d_A)$ is a compact metric space, if
   and only if for every family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$ with
   $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{U}$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with $A \subseteq U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n$,
   or else $A = \emptyset$.
3. **The same in indexed form.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$ if and only if
   for every set $I$ and every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$
   with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   indices $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with
   $A \subseteq U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, or else $A = \emptyset$.

Claim 3 is the form used by almost every later proof on this page, because a
cover is usually produced by a rule that attaches an open set to each point or to
each index, and a set of open sets forgets that rule. No choice principle is used
anywhere below; the one place a selection is made is over a finite index set, and
[[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim: Fix compact $K\subset X$. If $K$ is empty the conclusion is vacuous. Otherwise put $A_n=J_nS_n$ and $L=K\cup\bigcup_{n\ge1}A_n(K)$. The maps $A_n$ are continuous and converge uniformly on $K$ to the identity. Thus [F1] makes $L$ compact in the actual $X$ norm. By hypothesis $\sup_{b\in L}\|H_n(b)-H(b)\|_U\to0$.

In the concrete branch $0\le h_n<\infty$. If $h_n=0$, every cell is its singleton tag, so their finite union $D$ is finite. A nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$ contains a ball and hence infinitely many points; therefore this case forces $d=0$ and $D=\bar D$ is the singleton of $\mathbb R^0$. All tags are that point, and $J_n(z)(x)=z_1$ is a bounded linear reconstruction of norm at most one, with $J_nS_n(a)=a$ and reconstruction error $0=\omega_a(0)$. Now suppose $h_n>0$. Every point of $D$ is within $h_n$ of some tag in its cell. The distance to the finite tag set is continuous, so the same inequality holds on $\bar D$. Consequently $\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)>0$ there. The normalized weights are continuous, nonnegative and sum to one. Thus $J_n$ is a bounded linear map from the finite sample space with its maximum norm into $C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$, of norm at most one. The sampling map is bounded with norm at most one. A positive weight implies $|x-\xi_{n,j}|<2h_n$, so $\|J_nS_n(a)-a\|_\infty\le\omega_a(2h_n)$, where $\omega_a(r)=\sup_{|x-y|\le r}|a(x)-a(y)|$.

Continuity of $H$ controls uniform perturbations of the compact set $K$. Explicitly, for $\varepsilon>0$ collect every ball $B(x,r)$ with $x\in K$ and $r>0$ such that $\|H(z)-H(x)\|_U<\varepsilon/2$ for $\|z-x\|_X<3r$. These balls cover $K$; choose a finite subcover and take $\delta$ to be its smallest radius. If $a\in K$ and $\|b-a\|_X<\delta$, both points lie within $3r$ of one selected center, so $\|H(b)-H(a)\|_U<\varepsilon$. Hence $\sup_K\|H(A_n(a))-H(a)\|_U\to0$. Combining this with step 1.1 gives $\sup_K\|G_n-H\|_U\to0$. The maps $S_n$, identity on $E_n$, and $R_n=H_nJ_n$ provide the asserted finite-dimensional factorization, and [F4] applies when its function-space conventions hold; no access to the original input is used by $R_n$.

For a compact $K\subset C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$ and $\eta>0$, [F3] gives a finite $\eta$-net $a_1,\ldots,a_s$. By [F2] their moduli tend to zero. For $a\in K$ within $\eta$ of $a_i$, $\omega_a(r)\le2\eta+\omega_{a_i}(r)$. Therefore $\sup_{a\in K}\omega_a(r)\to0$. Step 1.2 supplies the reconstruction hypotheses of steps 1.1–2.1 and proves the whole concrete branch. The general argument measured every reconstruction error in $X$ and every output error in $U$, so it also proves the first clause without any unproved norm upgrade.

For the last assertion set $E_n=F_n=(\mathbb R^{q_0})^{N_n}$ and let $S_n(a)$ be its prescribed sample vector. For $z\in E_n$, construct $v_{1,n}(z)(x)=\sum_j\omega_{n,j}\kappa_n(x,\xi_{n,j})P(z_j)+b_n(x)$ and apply the subsequent raw stages to this field; call the resulting output $R_n(z)$. The first field belongs to its designated auxiliary space because it is a finite sum of its kernel sections and bias with finite scalar/vector coefficients. Every subsequent field belongs to its designated space by the stated compatibility assumptions. The finite sum and continuity of the lift make the first field continuous in $z$, and continuity of the subsequent maps makes $R_n:E_n\to U$ continuous. Induction through those stages proves $H_n(a)=R_n(S_n(a))$ exactly. The identity finite map between $E_n$ and $F_n$ gives [F4], and the assumed compact-uniform raw limit proves its convergence in the actual $U$ norm. No off-grid original input is requested at any stage of this construction.

citations.quote:
Let $A$ and $U$ be real Banach spaces of functions on bounded domains $D$ and $D'$, with the input point evaluations used below defined. For every $n\ge1$, choose finite-dimensional normed spaces $E_n,F_n$, an exactly defined sampling map $S_n:A\to E_n$ (for example, $S_n(a)=(a(\xi_{n,1}),\ldots,a(\xi_{n,N_n}))$ at specified input points), a finite-dimensional map $\widetilde G_n:E_n\to F_n$, and an output reconstruction map $R_n:F_n\to U$. The reconstruction supplies a function with a defined value at every point of $D'$. The corresponding continuum-valued discrete map is
$$G_n(a):=R_n\bigl(\widetilde G_n(S_n(a))\bigr)\in U.$$
A family $(G_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a **discretization-invariant approximation** of an operator $G:A\to U$ if its sampling maps and output reconstructions are part of the family and it approximates this single continuum operator as the input discretization is refined. In the compact-uniform version, for every compact $K\subset A$,
$$\sup_{a\in K}\|G_n(a)-G(a)\|_U\longrightarrow0.$$
For $K=\emptyset$, the supremum of this nonnegative error is defined to be $0$. When $A$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes, the sampling map must be explicitly defined on those classes or use a specified representative convention; point evaluation is not inferred from the equivalence class alone. This definition does not identify unrelated grid-specific maps as one operator family.

derivations.claim: For the specified layer, the continuum operator and every raw quadrature map are $H(a)=H_n(a)=a$: the integral term is zero, so replacing it by any tagged sum changes nothing. In particular, an arbitrary output query still asks for $a(x)$ in the local term.

The zero function and the polynomial $a(x)=\prod_{j=1}^N(x-\xi_j)^2$ have the same zero sample vector. The polynomial is not identically zero: any point of the interval outside the finite sampling set has strictly positive value. For $N=0$ use the empty product $a=1$. Thus their raw outputs differ by step 1.1. Any output reconstruction of the common finite vector would give them the same output by [F2], a contradiction. This disproves exact factorization of the raw rule. It asserts no obstruction to a reconstruction that only approximates the input, or to the separate compact-uniform quadrature convergence theorem.
